You will get a super-clean final build out of the Maestro 900R, and it will look stunning for the most part. But when you get up close, there are some parts which don't feel totally premium, and the price is as much of a barrier as the tempered glass side panels are to actually getting to your system's I/O ports.

PC Gamer's got your back Our experienced team dedicates many hours to every review, to really get to the heart of what matters most to you. Find out more about how we evaluate games and hardware.

It's just me in the office today. Normally that's fine. I don't mind the quiet, and I can be as messy as I like without Jacob tutting at me. Today is different. Today that comes with a healthy dose of fear. Fear because I have to lift the MSI Maestro 900R case up onto the test bench desk, and I don't think Paul, the oddball security guard way downstairs at the front desk, will hear me if I scream because my spine has snapped. It's a two person job and I'm very much a one-person team in PC Gamer towers today. I have managed to get it situated on the desk, but I can certainly feel it in my near fifty-year-old back muscles. *Spasm*. And when you need another human on hand every time you want to shift your gaming PC about, I think that says a lot about both this MSI case and who it's aimed at.

In short, I think you need to be someone who has their own staff.

That's partly a dig at its sheer scale—this thing is chomk with a capital CHOMK—but also at the fact only the very wealthy are going to consider this chassis a worthwhile casing for their gaming PC. This is a $700 (£800) PC case and that feels, on one hand, par for the course in these days of hyper-expensive everything, but also faintly anachronistic.

As always with the case reviewing process, I built a new PC inside it, and it only felt right to be doing so with high-end gear. So, I picked from the review kit that was in the cupboard: a MSI Godlike X with a Ryzen 9 9950X3D seemed appropriate, along with some 64 GB of G.Skill ULL memory and an RTX 5090. And that's when this whole endeavour started to feel like something from a bygone age.

Before, when I'd do a high-end build, it felt exciting in a way that was both special—because I could never spend out on such premium parts myself—but also still kind of achievable, too, because the money wasn't so far beyond the realms of decency that you couldn't imagine someone normal pushing their budget a little far to get this sort of kit. But looking at the parts going into this, it's around $12,000 worth of kit at least. And that feels well beyond a normal PC gamer and into faintly distasteful territory.

But, in all honesty, I'm not even totally convinced the MSI Maestro 900R really deserves its place in such company. Sure, it's elegant in black and gold trim, but there are odd touches here and there which belie the super premium pricing. The most egregious is something I picked out when I saw a preview case out at Computex this year, and that's the top flair on the case. The metal 'lid' only covers half of the dust filter for the 360 mm cooler I'd mounted to the top, and that filter is just a flimsy plastic one I wouldn't really want on display.

I also question the utility of having the motherboard and GPU's outputs all out of reach in the centre of the case, behind tempered glass shields. There are a ton of Type-A and Type-C USB ports on the front panel, but still it's a lot of effort to get to the I/O panel of your motherboard. And don't get me started on the PSU buried right in the back of the case, with impossible-to-reach switches and plug sockets.

The PC Gamer Circuit Breaker newsletter breaks down the latest PC gaming tech, and finds you the best deals on the best products

But there are things I like, too. The wraparound glass does look great, and I loved having so much space to work in when building into the rig. And to have that full central motherboard tray be completely removable was a treat, as well. You essentially have your own little test rig there, so you can make sure everything works before you do the full install. It's neat. As is the final build.

But honestly, this feels more like a chassis you might buy for someone else to build into. Because you're Mr. or Mrs. Moneybags and don't want to get your hands dirty doing manual labour and just want to have a high-end rig to play your games on in something that stands like a glass and gold monolith in the bespoke gaming room of your palace.

✅ You only have a passing knowledge of what's in your bank account: If you watch the pennies this isn't a chassis for you, but if you don't—and you're into the black, glass, and gold aesthetic, and have the space—then maybe it's worth considering.

❌ You need regular access to your mobo's I/O panel: The Maestro 900R hides it all away inside the case, meaning you have to open it up to get at the back of your motherboard.

You will get a super-clean final build out of the Maestro 900R, and it will look stunning for the most part. But when you get up close there are some parts which don't feel totally premium, and the price is as much of a barrier as the tempered glass side panels are to actually getting to your system's I/O ports.

Regular: E-ATX / ATX / Micro-ATX / Mini-ITX

1 x LED Switch Button · 1 x Mic-in / Audio-out · 1 x Power Button · 4 x USB 5Gbps (Type-A) · 4 x USB 10Gbps (Type-C) · 1 x USB 20Gbps (Type-C)

Top: 4 x 120 mm / 3 x 140 mm / 3 x 160 mm · Side: 6 x 120 mm · Bottom: 4 x 120 mm / 3 x 140 mm / 3 x 160 mm

Top: 120 / 140 / 240 / 280 / 360 / 420 mm · Side: 120 / 240 / 360 mm · Bottom: 120 / 140 / 240 / 280 / 360 / 420 mm

695 x 379 x 671 mm / 27.36 x 14.92 x 26.42 inches

Net weight: 33 kg / 72.75 lbs · Gross weight: 38 kg / 83.78 lbs

The key things to note are the sheer size of this beast. At well over 30 kilos, this is a massive chassis and when you've built a rig into it, that weight only goes up. It's a two-person job shifting this thing around, as my poor back can attest to.

The other thing is that it is really pleasing to build into. Thanks, in part, to the size of the case and the space you have to work in, but also because of that central motherboard tray. It is effectively a standalone test bench, and makes putting the board itself in place a doddle. It's also rotatable, so you can orient your system inside however you'd like. And because all the external cables need to be routed around from inside to outside anyways, you don't have to worry about where the mobo's I/O is going to go because it'll largely be inaccessible anyways.

To help this you have four 10 Gbps Type-C USB ports on the front of the case, along with a further 20 Gbps Type-C with 60 W power delivery, and four 5 Gbps USB Type-A ports. That does salve some of the pain of not being able to access your motherboard's back panel.

The other useful thing is that it comes with three 160 mm reverse blade fans, so the intakes on the base don't show their ugly side and ruin the high-end aesthetic.

Installation is an absolute joy… until it isn't. That occurs towards the end of the build, but at the start it really is all fun and games. The removable fan tray makes it easy to get your 360 mm radiator in place and the scale of the case means there's always space to work in when you've pulled the tool-free side panels off.

That motherboard tray is excellent, too. I was a big fan of that when I saw it out at Computex, and have been just as impressed now I've used it properly. The issue is that if you want to test out the components you've bought for this build using it as a standalone test bench, you will have to largely break it all down again before you can jam it into the system itself. But that's to be expected, and being able to just get your motherboard, CPU, cooling bracket, SSD, and RAM in place free from even the modest constraints of this massive rig is a real boon.

The installation pain is rear-loaded, however, and once you've got everything inside and wired up internally it then becomes a game of figuring out how the hell you're actually going to attach this thing up to either power or a monitor. There is no real back to this case, with the wraparound tempered glass surrounding the entire plane you mount the motherboard too. That means all the cables, from power, to display, to networking and anything else going into the back of your board, need to be routed out of some grommeted holes on the underside of the case.

It means you'll likely need a longer HDMI or DP cable than you have right now, because it needs to be routed in and around the inside of the case to get to the vertically mounted graphics card, which cuts a lot off its length. And you're unlikely to be sitting this on a desktop given its girth, so it's going to need to stretch from the ground up. Similarly, the power cable for the PSU has to be squeezed into the case, and if you're using a large PSU—such as the MSI MEG Ai1600T brick I've been using—then that doesn't give you a lot of space to attach its fat plug.

But that lack of a busy, cable-heavy backside to the case does really aid the aesthetic. The shroud (which is sadly quite flimsy plastic) that covers the rear of the vertically mounted GPU and the rear of the motherboard hides all the cables that sprout from their outputs as they're fed out the underside of the case, and that gives it a really clean finish. Inside, it looks like there is almost nothing connecting the components, leaving them looking like they're floating around inside. The MSI Godlike X motherboard only helped this by hiding a lot of its power cabling, too.

The angled reverse-bladed fans on the bottom intake are slightly angled, which allows you to see them in all their RGB LED glory, but that, coupled with the angling of the top radiator mount, makes it feel even bigger inside. I really like the full wraparound tempered glass, too. It really gives it a showpiece aesthetic, which I can see being used at a bunch of PC trade show booths in the future.

What slightly ruins that aesthetic, however, is the exposed plastic dust cover on the top of the case. The metal cover, which slots on without screws, only partially covers the things, leaving it open to be eyeballed. And it's not a great look. Likewise, the plastic shroud covering the cables inside looks and feels flimsy. It's the same with the power and LED buttons on the front panel. They look like they could have come from any $50 chassis, as does the lightbar on the rear side of the case's top.

It is not the most expensive PC chassis you can buy on Newegg right now. But that's mostly because Newegg's marketplace is an odd place to be and there are a ton of Hatsune Miku Asus cases on there with four-figure price tags, and I can't figure out why. There's also a $1,000 Asus ProArt chassis on there, but you can also just buy that for $300 direct from Newegg if you'd rather. Which is a roundabout way of me saying that it is pretty much the most expensive chassis you can buy on Newegg without delving into the murky realms of the marketplace.

And, personally, I find it hard to reconcile any notions of value against the MSI Maestro 900R beyond the sheer mass of the thing. Were we going by size and weight, then, I guess it's a match for the Asus ProArt PA602. That's half the weight and half the price, so on a purely per-gram metric, it's all evens Antoine Griezmanns.

But in real terms, it's a massive, expensive case, that I struggle to find genuine ways to justify its cost. There are some neat features, such as that mobo tray, but also some genuine points of frustration that would have me not actually wanting to clothe my PC parts in its black, gold, and glass surrounds. I'm happy with my—what seems to be rather diminutive now—Hyte Y70 Touch. Again, it's half the price, but at least I can get at my PC bits and not break my spine picking it up off the ground.

4. Best budget compact: Thermaltake S100 TG Snow Edition

You will get a super-clean final build out of the Maestro 900R, and it will look stunning for the most part. But when you get up close, there are some parts which don't feel totally premium, and the price is as much of a barrier as the tempered glass side panels are to actually getting to your system's I/O ports.

Now he's back, writing about the nightmarish graphics card market, CPUs with more cores than sense, gaming laptops hotter than the sun, and SSDs more capacious than a Cybertruck.

The anticipated remake of the seminal Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time dropped this week. Lifelong fans are returning to a familiar but altered Hyrule. The world originally rendered in 1998 has greater fidelity, hunkier non-playable characters, wiser chickens and, most notably, a jump button. For the regular player itâs a marvel and an adjustment. For speedrunners, itâs a tantalizing playground of tech to be discovered. As the weekend rolls out, and runners dredge the kingdom for secret exploits, theyâre establishing a potential blueprint for record times. As well as uncovering some bizarre horrors along the way.

To say The Legend of Zelda series has some abnormal tech is an understatement. Ever since Link stepped out of his treehouse into a 3D, polygonal world, it was clear the code that binds his reality had a soft underbelly. Ocarinaâs boomerang can rewrite item placement. Wind Wakerâs camera can launch little Toon Link into hyperspeed across the ocean. Skyward Swordâs opening menu seems to exist in some kind of temporal pocket dimension. Nintendoâs fine tuned games have always operated on peculiar physics, but for speedrunners, a return to Ocarina presents an opportunity to rewrite the playbook.

Ladies and gentlemen, we have a speedrun pic.twitter.com/hRN97USavV

The most obvious source for potential run-aiding glitches is Linkâs newfound ability to jump. Like in Breath of the Wild, Link no longer needs to run off a cliff to remember how to use his knees. In standard play, Link can go higher. Speedrunners want to see just how high he can go. Find unassuming geography that can act as shortcuts. Some of the classics, like the building-bounding ‘Hookshot Jump,’ appear to be viable. One of the most popular pieces of tech revolves around open chests. Now that Link can step into them, positioning his feet inside them at just the right angle seems to bristle the game, launching the player like a trampoline. Dropping a bomb in there seems to help as well.

Like previous Zelda games, plenty of glitches lay dormant outside of realtime play. Remake runners are already stress testing start menus and inventory to see what will happen when spammed and agitated. And sure enough, flipping between items in your inventory midair seems to cause Link to float like a leaf in the wind.

“This bug shouldn’t exist lol,” posted ORCinfo. “Once you get used to it, you can jump endlessly in midair. This is gonna break speedruns.”

Defying gravity is obviously useful, but potential sequence breaking exploits is what plummets a runtime from hours into minutes. Stumbling across the proper tech could allow players to skip items, temples, plot beats or reroute them into a more convenient order. This is especially prescient in a game that swaps between two different periods. As runner Zfg1 is chronicling, messing with the hero of time does seem to have a bit of a butterfly effect. While sadly temporary, triggering cut adult Link cutscenes as child Link, and vice versa, momentarily confuses the remake, scrunching his texture files into a neanderthal, or the product of coming out the other end of Amigara Fault.

We can now beat Shadow Temple as child, which automatically turns you into adult. We still have 1 roadblock to get past before this can be used in a speedrun, but it'll be huge assuming we can get past it.

It also looks very funny. pic.twitter.com/s2aoTKCQyY

The day is young as far as how any of this can be applied. Glitches can be awe inspiring, but if they donât contribute to faster runs theyâre just a party trick. Likewise seemingly benign exploits can sometimes pierce through to monumental discoveries, especially as run conditions become more niche. But things are moving fast, even for a scene preoccupied with being fast. The attention to a speedrunning classic means new glitches will be hitting hard and fast. And Link, poor Link, is along for the ride.

#3745. How to Export Your Arc Data to a New Browser

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

If you've been a dedicated Arc browser user, the time has finally come to say goodbye. The Browser Company paused development of Arc in 2025, continuing only with security updates. As announced late last week, Arc will officially sunset on Dec. 22, 2026, giving users two months to transition their data to an alternative.

One option is to move to the company's new AI-focused Dia browser, though there are other (potentially better) choices depending on what you're looking for. Most data from Arc—including Spaces, Favorites, pinned tabs, and folders as well as passwords, bookmarks, extensions, and history—will transition automatically over to Dia, but if you're switching to a different platform entirely, you'll need to take what you can with you before Dec. 22.

Officially, Arc supports exporting Spaces and tabs only, and the resulting Export.md plain-text file is simply a list of links that you can open and bookmark in your new browser. MacOS users can initiate this process via Arc > Settings > Advanced > Export Data and saving the file to a preferred location. On Windows, open the Arc menu, select Settings, and go to Export Spaces and tabs > Export Data.

To simply copy and paste every link from one folder, right-click the folder, select Copy All Links, and paste them wherever you'd like (select Copy All Links as Markdown to keep link titles on macOS). You can also save Easels as images by tapping the share icon > Share Via... and selecting PNG.

There's no formal process to export other Arc data. If you saved logins in Arc, now is a good time to start moving credentials over to a different platform. (Our top picks for password managers aren't tied to a single browser.)

There are a few alternatives to Arc's official export process, which is highly manual and doesn't keep your folder structure intact. There are several third-party scripts available (for free) that can facilitate the transition as well as a paid extension called ArcEscape that can export folders and pinned tabs and import into another browser. The extension is available for Chrome, Edge, Brave, Vivaldi, and Firefox. According to Arc's FAQ, all user accounts will be deactivated on Dec. 22, and personal data will be deleted within 30 days of deactivation.

#3744. "Art, including characters, terrain, animations, cutscenes and UI" Bandai Namco and Monolith Soft helped out with Ocarina of Time on Switch 2

Xenoblade series developer Monolith Soft and Bandai Namco Studios have been listed as support studios for the Switch 2 version of Ocarina of Time, working on elements of the title such as "art, including characters, terrain, animations, cutscenes and UI". Special thanks to both companies appear in the credits for the newly-launched game (as you can see below) and a statement released by Bandai Namco Studios confirms its involvement, too.

"We were commissioned to produce some of the visual assets and artwork, including characters, environments, animations, cutscenes, and UI elements, for The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, a Nintendo Switch 2 game released by Nintendo Co., Ltd. on 5th November, 2026," reads a translated release from Bandai Namco Studio reads.

Of course, this isn't the first time we've seen Bandai Namco Studios' talents leveraged to help with Nintendo games: the publisher and its internal studios worked closely with Nintendo as a co-developer on the long-awaited Metroid Prime 4, and we know the studios are listed as co-developer for first-party Switch 2 titles like Mario Kart World and Splatoon Raiders. Typically, the work carried out by Bandai Namco comes from one of two dedicated internal studios that are contracted specifically to work with Nintendo: Studio 2 and Studio S. You can see a full list of the games Bandai Namco's support studios have worked on here. You'll note there are many Nintendo first-party titles listed here, going back to 2012 and Mario Kart 8. In late 2025, Nintendo acquired Bandai Namco Studios Singapore from the publisher, renaming the company Nintendo Studios Singapore.

"Alongside great judgement and clever tweaks, this astonishing remake has a proper ace up its sleeve," wrote our reviewer, Christian Donlan, in his five-star review of the Switch 2 game last week. "This is Ocarina as it's always been, as timeless and intricate, but it also has a vibrancy and clarity that makes it feel like it was just created last Wednesday."

If - somehow! - you've already gobbled up most of the game and you're keen to play it again, you will be pleased to know that Master Quest code has been found in datamined files for the title, suggesting DLC may well be on the way in the not-too-distant future.

2024’s Deadpool & Wolverine was the realization of a dream for Channing Tatum, as he was finally able to debut his big screen character Gambit. Years before that, Tatum had been eager to play the fan-favorite X-Man and was to do so in a solo film. That flick ultimately didn’t pan out, but a lot of work was put in beforehand. Tatum recently recalled trying to get that comic book movie off the ground and, while doing so, he revealed one major mistake he could've made amid development.

Tatum was first linked to the role of cajun card thrower Remy LeBeau around 2014, at which point it was reported that he’d debut in 2016’s X-Men: Apocalypse before leading his own movie. He even promoted the film at Comic-Con in 2014. During a recent interview with ScreenRant, Tatum promoted Dunkin’ Donuts’ promotional campaign for the upcoming Avengers: Doomsday, in which he’ll reprise Remy. The Magic Mike alum was asked if a solo film centered around his character was still a possibility, and he didn’t strike down the idea.

However, if that X-Men spinoff were to happen, something Tatum wouldn’t be bullish about is directing himself, and that was something he aimed to do when he was developing the film years ago.

As the Magic Mike alum explained, he and his producing partner, Reid Carolin, were motivated to make the movie by “frustration and hubris,” and they went through quite a few directors:

We had three different directors that were signed up to do it, and the first one, the studio, Fox, they had a fallout, so that one didn't work out. The second one was just in development for so long with somebody that I was just like, ‘We got to move to making this thing.’ So we separated ourselves, and then the third one almost got going with Gore Verbinski, and then creatively all three of us, the studio, him and me, we started in the same place, and then as it developed, we just all grew apart.

Following all that, Tatum and Carolin apparently approached 20th Century Fox about commissioning a script “that the studio wanted to make, and that we wanted to make.” The hope was for that script to attract a filmmaker who would want to direct it as it was. However, after seeing the screenplay, the pair loved the script, and that passion fueled the idea that one of them helm the flick. That eagerness only grew after Shawn Levy – who, ironically, directed D&W years later – praised their script and expressed interest in helming Gambit.

Channing Tatum is now grateful to have not directed the movie, as it’s his belief that neither he nor Reid Carolin were prepared to direct a film of that scale. The Jump Street star even went so far as to say that the production “would've failed miserably” had he or Carolin helmed it. He also said this:

Now that I know exactly what directing is and how complicated it is and how these movies specifically are so hard, you really need to know what you're doing. It can't be your first movie. You've got to really get a lot of different facets under your belt and have a lot of experience because making one of these movies is nearly impossible. Some people really have the formula down and really know how to do it, and some others struggle. It would've just been a catastrophe on a level that I would never have recovered from.

I can certainly understand the concerns, especially considering how big a superhero movie can be. Tatum may have been “traumatized” by the movie not panning out, but it sounds like he learned a valuable lesson from the experience. Plus, it’s worth mentioning that Tatum has since made his directorial debut with the critically well received road dramedy Dog, which hit theaters in 2022.

Tatum is also blessed in that he’s still in the position to play Gambit, who delighted audiences (and Ryan Reynolds) with his sick moves and thick cajun accent. Based on the Dunkin’ ad, Remy’s cadence may be a bit more tame in Doomsday. I’m not sure if Tatum’s version of LeBeau will appear beyond the team-up film, especially due to the upcoming X-Men reboot. But, if the door of opportunity swings open, Tatum will walk through it, even if he doesn’t seem keen on directing.

Avengers: Doomsday opens in theaters on December 18 amid the 2026 movie schedule. Fans can also check out Channing Tatum’s performance as Gambit in Deadpool & Wolverine by streaming the film with a Disney+ subscription.

#3742. Melty New Puzzle Game From Shotgun King Creators Burns Tetris At Both Ends

Game JamIndie GamesLudum DarePuzzleTetris

You live through life fending off all kinds of intrusive thoughts. Resisting the urge to kick every tire icicle. Plucking at grass, which wasnât bothering no one. Lighting a really tall candle and giving it a nudge just to make sure it couldnât possibly fall over otherwise. A new game from the creators of Shotgun King will free you of those inhibitions. A reimagining of Tetris that demands that you ignite the wick right through to the stem. As much as Hot Wax latches itself to an impulse, it still demands you carefully consider your next move, lest you burn yourself out later.

Presented deep within some unilluminated, dungeon keep, Hot Wax has you kicking off a summoning ritual with the use of magical candles. While tetromino shaped, these blocks do not extinguish themselves upon forming a horizontal line. Instead they must be burned from the top down. Every couple of pieces, the player is given a small ball of fire, which will carry along the path of the candle. Lighting any other exposed twine it brushes up against. However, remaining blocks of wax will tumble down when separated, a la Mr. Driller, and the ember will be snuffed out if smothered. Leaving you with a big basin of impenetrable goo.

Hot Wax requires you to rewire your Tetris instincts. The default practice of neatly arranging your blocks is efficiency for efficiencyâs sake. What you really want to do is create a safe path for the ember to do as much arson as possible. The rules differ slightly between modes as well. In the standard ritual, the flame only progresses one block per turn, though there is an opportunity to nab devilish power ups. In other modes, the fire will scorch right through, not just an immediate gratification but a helpful visual aid for seeing the game logic in real time.

Created by Shotgun King developers PUNKCAKE Delicieux, Hot Wax was born out of a 2024 Ludum Dare game jam. Like Kingâs blasting of chess, Wax comes at Tetris from underneath. Taking the malleable shape of it and working it with its fingers. Itâs reminiscent of the early dreamscape days of the genre, where Pipe Dreams tried to put a blue collar spin on the hit, while Alexey Pajitnov himself wondered “What if I gave Tetris a fancy little hat.” Itâs a comfortable space for PUNKCAKE, who will be hitting word jumbles the same way with If Letters Had Pants, Would They Wear Them Like This?

#3740. Skyrim lead designer hopes Sentinel will finally solve The Elder Scrolls' ladder problem

For such a simple, straightforward real-world object, ladders have been the bane of game developers' existence since the early days of the industry. And Bethesda's The Elder Scrolls Series is certainly no stranger to that struggle.

While we may be years away from the release of The Elder Scrolls 6: Sentinel, the recent title reveal reignited conversations about what longtime fans hope to see from it. That includes former Bethesda developers, such as Skyrim lead designer and Bethesda veteran Bruce Nesmith, who picked ladders as one thing he hopes Sentinel actually figures out.

If you're unfamiliar, ladders in Skyrim work in a weird way. You don't animatedly climb up and down them, but rather the character simply teleports from one end to the other. Speaking to The Examined Game (via GamesRadar+), Nesmith said that Skyrim's approach "really limits the art team in terms of how you can do multi-layer [levels]".

"It seems simple, it seems stupid, but you don't climb up and down ladders," said Nesmith. "All the ladders in Skyrim, you click on the ladder, poof, you're at the top or you have to climb a stair.

"But to do ladders, you have to deal with a whole host of questions which our programmers very legitimately put in front of us and said, 'You give me answers to these, I'll tell you how much programming time it's going to take to make them.' And you know, that caused problems right there."

Nesmith then pointed out the hidden complexity of creating functioning ladders in games, and the scenarios developers have to anticipate and account for, especially in a game as dynamic as an Elder Scrolls title.

"So, I'm halfway up a ladder, and [an] NPC decides to climb down it. What happens?" Nesmith posited. "The NPC has to have AI that will adjust for that. Does the player go through the NPC? Is he blocked by the NPC? Does the NPC stay on the ladder? Does the NPC go back up and know to wait and then come back down?

"And I'm just scratching the surface of some of the problems they brought up. So, it seems simple, and other games have climbing ladders, but we chose to put our efforts into other things to make them better rather than deal with that. So, I'd like to see Bethesda finally come around to making ladders a reality where you're actually climbing them and make the world feel a little more immersive."

While we know very little about Sentinel right now - much less how it's going to solve the ladder problem -that hasn't stopped fans from speculating about a number of topics, including what they believe is going to be a split / alternate timeline setup.

If you have a high-end RTX 50-series graphics card then kudos to you. You either got in there early and avoided the massive price hikes that followed, or you managed to get a second mortgage and pick one up anyways. But either way, you're going to want to protect your investment because replacements are hard and expensive to find. And it looks like you really need to protect that investment because there are still regular cases of melting 12+4 pin power cables.

This latest (via Uniko's Hardware) serves as a reminder that getting a cable monitoring solution is a good way to protect your expensive graphics card, as user Edistonian2 notes in a recent reddit thread on the ThermalGrizzly sub. They note that they picked up an RTX 5090 in June and subsequently grabbed a WireView Pro II monitor to keep it safe.

The WireView noted odd current behaviour with two of the pins, while HWInfo said it was fine and a Gemini chat suggested it was an issue with the monitor. I'm sure that's what Nvidia would say, too... So they replace their WireView with a new one, and still get the current issues on pin four. So they removed the cable entirely and the image up top is what was happening on the PSU end of the wire.

They've since picked up another cable and swapped to the other GPU power port on the GPU and so far everything is fine, but it just shows that there are still power issues going on with these cables and a monitoring system can be a worthwhile step in between finding your power leads or plugs melting, or your GPU going up in a puff of smoke.

Now, it's not the cheapest method—the WireView Pro II is $190 at Amazon right now—but that is chump change in relation to the ~$8,000 you might have to spend on a replacement RTX 5090. There are also cheaper alternatives, such as Cooler Master's GPU Shield, which is $50, and the Super Flower 12+4 pin OCP Dongle.

Whichever you choose, as the pricing crisis continues for high-end cards, that's going to be a small price to pay to save something catastrophic happening to your expensive silicon.

#3737. Nintendo's legendary Kirby designer Masahiro Sakurai weighs in on gen-AI, saying "it has yet to gain my trust" but not to reject it completely

"Doing nothing is probably not the right approach."

Masahiro Sakurai, the designer behind many iconic Nintendo franchises such as Super Smash Bros. and several Kirby titles, has weighed in on the ongoing discussion of generative-AI use in game development.

At an event celebrating the release of his new book - Masahiro Sakurai’s Thoughts on Games - the veteran director told Famitsu he hasn't and currently isn't using the technology to make games, noting that the role of a designer is to generate ideas.

"It has yet to gain my trust," Sakurai said via DeepL machine translation. Regarding graphical use specifically, he added that, "It must not amount to exploitation of any kind," and that "for the time being, we can produce better results by coming up with ideas ourselves".

But Sakurai is wary of rejecting gen-AI completely, saying "making games today is far too difficult", with some games "running at a loss even after selling millions of copies". A company in that position may go under if it does not change its stance on generative-AI, he suggested. "Doing nothing is probably not the right approach," he said, but "where and how to use it" is a complex topic with a lot of uncertainties. Sakurai is taking "a slow-paced approach" for now.

Outside of regular industry layoffs, the use of generative-AI in games has been the most controversial topic amongst developers and players. Some argue it's already being used in multiple development disciplines, notably programming and writing code. Others, such as Shigeru Miyamoto, are more sceptical of the technology's capabilities, especially when it comes to the more creative and art-driven parts of game development.

#3735. 10 Hacks Every Google Messages User Should Know

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

Google Messages is Google's official texting app, and while it hasn't always been first to roll out useful features, it has caught up to what other messaging services offer and has a handful of hidden hacks to make communicating and coordinating with contacts easier and safer. Here are the best tips and tricks that every Google Messages user should know.

Google Messages recently got a Google Keep integration, which allows group chat participants to collaborate on notes and checklists directly in the message thread without having to click over to a separate app. This also centralizes ideas in one place rather than spread across a thread with dozens of separate text messages. Changes to Keep Notes sync automatically for all users. Tap the plus icon in the message compose bar in Google Messages, select Keep Notes, and either choose an existing note or tap to create a new one to be shared in the chat.

Over the last few years, Google has rolled out a number of security features for identifying and defending against scams and fraud spread via calls and text messages. These work by detecting suspected spam and either preventing it from being delivered or hiding it in a separate folder, as well as flagging suspicious links. A newer opt-in enhanced protection mode for Google Messages uses AI to catch more complex threats and alert you if a conversation or unfamiliar link that looks legit might put you at risk. Standard protection is on by default, but you can turn on enhanced protection under Messages settings > Protection & Safety > Spam and scam protection.

If you have an idea you want to write down but not send immediately—because it's outside of work hours or late at night—you can draft it in Google Messages and schedule it for later. "Send later" features in messaging and chat apps are useful for maintaining good boundaries without having to remember to type and send at a different time. Once you've entered your message in the text field, touch and hold Send, choose from the suggested actions, then tap Send again.

Swiping left or right on your conversations in Google Messages will either archive or delete them. You can customize which swipe maps onto which action for quick inbox triaging or disable one or both to prevent accidentally triggering an unwanted action. Tap your profile photo > Message settings > Swipe actions > Customize to select your preferences.

Google Messages has a pinning feature that will anchor conversations at the top of your message history, but you can also star important messages you want to save and return to later. Starring makes it easy to keep track of data like flight information, contacts, or dates that might otherwise get lost in a thread or be difficult to pull up in a basic search—starred messages have their own search filter. Simply tap and hold the message and tap Star at the top, then go to Search conversations > Starred > More options > Starred to see your list of saved messages.

We've all been in the overactive group chat that we don't want to see notifications from in real time but also don't want to leave. You can snooze threads semi-permanently, but you can also turn on a temporary snooze that will lift so notifications restart after a short period of time. This can be useful for threads discussing live events or games you will be catching up on later or if you need silence during a focused work period. Touch and hold the conversation, tap Snooze, then select your duration and tap Snooze to confirm. You can choose from 1 hour, 8 hours, 24 hours, or always.

Google Messages has two group chat modes. Group MMS is your typical group text—it sends a single message to all recipients, and everyone receives replies in the thread. Mass Text, by contrast, is like BCC. This sends your message to each user individually, and replies come only to the original sender. Using this mode allows you to share information with a bunch of people at once without creating the dreaded reply-all thread. You can change your default group messaging settings via profile > Message settings > Advanced > Group messaging.

Google Messages finally launched integrated real-time location sharing earlier this year, which allows you to send your live whereabouts to trusted contacts directly in a message thread. Location sharing makes it easier to coordinate meeting up or let someone know where you are if there are any safety concerns. You can set a limited duration or leave location sharing on indefinitely for specific contacts. Open a conversation and tap Attachment > Real-time location

You don't have to live with the embarrassment of sending a text in error with Google Messages—at least not if you catch the mistake quickly. Google Messages has a "Delete for everyone" function that can remove sent messages from the devices of users who are running the latest version of the app. Conversations must be using RCS for this to work, and you have only a limited window—anywhere from 15 to 40 minutes, according to support documentation—to use the feature before your messages are permanent. Long-press a message to pull up available delete options.

If you want to stay on top of your text threads but get distracted by other things every time you pick up your phone, you can log into the Google Messages web interface on your browser. This also makes it easier to send photos and files from your computer via Google Messages without having to transfer them to your phone first.

#3734. Activision cracking down on popular Call of Duty: Warzone app that basically constituted cheating

"Lobby shopping" is what Call of Duty: Warzone players have been calling the ability to check the skill level of players in a lobby prior to joining it, enabling them to pass on those that include a lot of tough competition.

There are several ways players, notably Twitch streamers and content creators, have been able to do that over the years. But the use of one app in particular - Warzone Agent - has been considered by many to be cheating, and Activision is finally doing something about it.

Alongside the launch of Modern Warfare 4's version of Warzone and the game's first season of post-launch content, Call of Duty's anti-cheat team Ricochet has announced it's officially cracking down on Warzone Agent.

"Yesterday, we began taking action against Warzone Agent, a paid, unauthorised third party tool that lets users lobby shop in Warzone," the developer revealed in a post on X. "Ricochet anti-cheat will block players attempting to load the software and instruct them to unload it before accessing multiplayer."

Having the ability to cherrypick the lobby with the lowest-skilled players possible bypasses the game's matchmaking algorithm, potentially ruining the game for the dozens of other players in the match. Historically, content creators have used the app (and other methods) to post impressive kill records.

The developer added in a follow-up message that: "Using unauthorised software to manipulate the player experience violates Activision terms of use and leaves your account and hardware subject to enforcement." The language seems to stop just short of outright confirming those players using Warzone Agent will be banned.

As part of this crackdown, Ricochet reiterated its stance on boosting - artificially increasing (or decreasing) one's skill rating - saying that it too is considered cheating. "Receiving a boost, having another player log in to boost your account, or purchasing a boosted account are all against policy," the developer said.

"Boosting services flood lobbies with low effort accounts used to farm XP and complete challenges. Those accounts can later be sold as Ranked Play ready, directly feeding the cheating marketplace."

More than 20,000 boosting-related accounts have been removed since the launch of Modern Warfare 4, according to the developer, and Ricochet will "continue to apply pressure" in this area.

The quality of multiplayer was a particular highlight in Eurogamer's review of Modern Warfare 4, in which Dom Peppiatt lauded the complexity of weapon handling, which works without taking away from accessibility of the gunplay.

Skyrim lead designer Bruce Nesmith had a wide-ranging chat with The Examined Game recently, touching upon topics like the importance of institutional knowledge, what he liked about Baldur's Gate 3, and what he wants to see in The Elder Scrolls 6: Sentinel. But he also dropped a pithy maxim (and less pithy explanation) about his—and Bethesda's—approach to design in general. Here's what he said.

"If you look at the history of triple-A studios that do sequels… you'll see the best game in a sequence frequently was able to maintain a vision, and was very player-centric-forward: 'You're not playing my game, I'm making your game' kind of thing.

One of the things I've always felt, and [Bethesda] felt it too [is] once we've made a game, it's not ours anymore. It's yours. I, once upon a time, actually had a developer complain to me that the people playing his game—it wasn't anything Bethesda produced—were playing it wrong.

I immediately told him, 'they're not playing it wrong, they cannot play it wrong, it's their game. It's not yours anymore. However they are choosing to play it is the right way to play it'... If you embrace that on the developer side, you find yourself making all different kinds of content, both artistically and design, and for programming in terms of the systems that are available, so that everyone can play the game the way they want to".

I'm not sure I've ever heard a more succinct summation of the Bethesda school of game design than "You're not playing my game, I'm making your game". Accessibility, openness, a sanding down of edges that may scare off the normies (like ability scores and character classes—gone but not forgotten), and a general refusal to foreclose story branches or quest chains based on player decisions: these things are Bethesda to me.

In this maxim you find all the strengths and weaknesses of the studio's approach to open-world RPG design. On the one hand, the world is your oyster. If a questline is losing your interest, flip to another one. Don't like your build? Convert to something new. Bethesda's worlds are all-you-can-eat buffets and you have precisely zero dietary restrictions. True freedom!

And yet, and yet, to a certain kind of tedious grognard (me), it also leaves everything feeling a touch… limp—colourless in content and utterly unresponsive. You might be the head of every guild in the land and the bloodletter-in-chief of the local murder society, but the world is too shy to reply to it. After all, it can't. If your choices impacted things too hard you might experience a consequence, you might rub up against a rough edge, and then suddenly you might not be playing "your" game anymore.

#3731. 10 Shows Like 'VisionQuest' You Should Watch Next

Ross Johnson writes about television, film, and literature for Lifehacker. He has a degree in political science from the University of Rochester and has previously been a legal writer and editor for Thomson Reuters, for which he later traveled around India and the Middle East as an educator specializing in American English style and grammar for adults.

Ross has been an actor on stage, in commercials, and in independent films since childhood, and has written hundreds of articles and essays on genre literature and cinema for Barnes & Noble, Gizmodo, Kotaku, and Yahoo! Entertainment.Ross produces the Swan Songs film podcast and hosts The Sound of Tomorrow, a pop culture and current affairs radio show based in Rochester, New York, where he lives with his husband and dogs and supports the local arts and cinema scene. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Following the events of WandaVision (and, slightly more tangentially, Agatha All Along), VisionQuest returns to the story of Marvel's favorite synthic being, an artificial creation who fights supervillains and ponders the nature of his own existence, rather than more typical AI pursuits like creating deep fakes.

White Vision (the character, not the political agenda) is a copy of the Vision who died two Avengers movies ago. He's living within his own mind on a fantasy country estate while on the run from bounty hunters and in pursuit of his semi-fictional son. In that spirit, here are 10 more science fiction shows that involve artificial people and/or elaborate constructed realities.

In the near-future world, highly advanced “synths” are commonplace, doing the work that regular humans can’t be bothered with. These beings are treated as entirely disposable sources of cheap labor, despite their apparent burgeoning humanity. The first season introduces the Hawkins family, who buy (on sale) a domestic servant synth named Anita (Gemma Chan); mom Laura is a little uncomfortable with the arrangement, especially when she finds her husband having sex with Anita, who has her own complicated backstory. Humans interrogates the ways humans always seem to find excuses to dehumanize others, which is just the type of thing that sci-fi is pretty great at. Stream Humans on Peacock, Prime Video, and Tubi.

One of the smartest recent shows is a dark comedy based on the Hugo-Award winning book series by Martha Wells. Alexander Skarsgård is the title's hilariously deadpan robot, a private "security construct" who's managed to hack its way through its own programming and gain free will—which it mostly wants to use to binge its favorite streaming shows. It can't just run off for fear of drawing attention, but the self-named Murderbot (it's being ironic, kinda) is content to do the bare minimum when it's assigned to a team of naive hippie researchers who don't see the need for a killer security robot—at least, not until they're enmeshed in a complicated capitalist plot in which they're all just cogs. Stream Murderbot on Apple TV.

From playwright Tearrance Arvelle Chisholm (Hooded: Or Being Black for Dummies), this show stars Okieriete Onaodowan as the title character, an inhabitant of an alternate present who is turning 33 and pursuing therapy for the first time. He's offered the chance to use DIRT (Digital Immersive Reality Therapy), in which he can visit and view other versions of himself, as long as he doesn't interfere. Which, of course, he does, with results that are sometimes poignant and sometimes funny. Hard to believe that this clever show almost wound up in the bin, a victim of that stupid moment a couple of years ago when streamers and studios were shelving otherwise great projects for tax reasons. No robots here, but a human exploring a complex world inside his own head. Stream Demascus on Tubi.

In this more darkly dangerous vision of a virtual world, video-game-obsessed Arisu gets his wish, after a fashion; he finds himself, along with a couple of friends, transported to an alternate, eerily abandoned version of Tokyo—the title’s Borderland—vividly brought to life via clever green screen work. The three are directed to an arena and given the instructions for the game, which they’ll be playing whether they want to or not. The first competition involves a locked-room-style puzzle; if they fail, the room goes up in flames with them in it—think Ready Player One, with deadlier stakes. There are games each night, though the rules allow for winners to get time off. There are a lot of rules, actually, but the games are cleverly and sadistically constructed. Stream Alice in Borderland on Netflix.

Though ostensibly an X-Men spinoff, this phantasmagoric show from Noah Hawley (Fargo, Alien: Earth) stands entirely on its own, taking place largely inside the headspace of a deeply troubled man. Dan Stevens plays David Haller, diagnosed with schizophrenia and possessed of tremendous psychic abilities. In one of the many psychiatric hospitals to which he's been committed, he meets first the free-wheeling Lenny (Aubrey Plaza) and then Syd (Rachel Keller), who can trade bodies with anyone she touches. Veering in and out of trippy astral planes and deeply damaged psyches, David soon comes to realize that he's not crazy—and also that he's probably not the hero of the story, even as he's caught between the authorities who'd like to use him for his power and the Shadow King who's been haunting his mind since childhood. Stream Legion on Hulu.

Just a science fiction action comedy about a nun married to literal Jesus on a quest to save the world from the title's artificial intelligence by finding the Holy Grail alongside her ex-boyfriend. So, yeah, there’s a lot going on in Mrs. Davis—sometimes a little too much, but the show gets major points for ambition. Betty Gilpin holds everything together as Sister Simone, playing it straight in an extremely over-the-top world. It’s refreshing to see a show that’s so unafraid to take big swings, and it works much more often than it should. Though it was cancelled after one season, it ends reasonably well, and, like co-creator Damon Lindelof’s HBO series Watchmen, would probably be best served by remaining a one-and-done. Stream Mrs. Davis on Peacock.

A charming comedy-drama set in a science fiction world, Robbie Amell stars as Nathan Brown, a young computer programmer who's also recently deceased. In the future of 2033, humans have the option of having their consciousnesses uploaded into virtual worlds post-mortem and Nathan's is chosen for him by his rich and rather possessive girlfriend. The exclusive afterlife setting of Lakeview is stifling, as is the fact that said girlfriend has a say in his perpetual existence. He's on the brink of despair until he strikes up a friendship with Nora (Andy Allo), his very-much-alive customer service rep. Stream Upload on Prime Video and Hulu.

Tricky to recommend, given that the show's four seasons saw a period of decline followed by a cancellation just when it was getting really good again—however, when Westworld was cooking (as in its addictive first season), there was nothing else like it on television. Set, initially, in a high-tech, near-future amusement park designed to appeal to wealthy clientele, the show finds the lifelike androids created to service the guests gradually waking up to their disposability. In the best tradition of sci-fi, this one's less about AI than it is about a world of disposable beings existing purely at the whim, and for the amusement of, the ultra-wealthy. Which is definitely not a 100% relatable metaphor. Buy Westworld from Prime Video.

You've likely seen this one if you're watching VisionQuest, but it's worth mentioning as not only a fairly essential preface, but also one of the best (and most distinctive) bits of Marvel media...ever? (Agatha All Along is also great, but less essential to Vision's narrative). At least initially, WandaVision confused dedicated Marvel fans as much as noobs, making it a unique on-ramp, even if it does have many threads connected to the broader superhero universe. Its story of a grieving witch living out her sitcom fantasies is an impressive swing into the surreal, well worth it if you’re content to go along for a weird and surprisingly emotional ride. Stream WandaVision on Disney+.

#3730. Return Of The Living Dead Cast Horrified By AI-Made Sequel They Were Originally Set To Star In

Last weekend was Halloween. A night for creeps. An evening of shrieks. For some scream queen royalty, they got one of the more unpleasant kinds of frights. Richard Driscoll, who crowdfunded a sequel to the 1985 punk zombie classic Return of the Living Dead, published the new film on his website. This came to the surprise to the original cast, who were attached to star in the follow-up. Instead it seems Driscoll opted to use AI to generate the film, leaving fans and alumni more aghast at him than the flesh eating ghouls.

“This is not what we signed up for,” says Beverly Randolph on the Caffeinated Horror Dude podcast. “We got to get something out there because there’s so much hate on us right now.”

Due to some erroneous paperwork, George A. Romeroâs original Night of the Living Dead was released directly into the public domain in 1968. Because of this, it enabled any director and studio, including Romero himself, to develop âsequelsâ to the series regardless of legal claim. One of the more adored successors is Return of the Living Dead, where a gang of punk teenagers take refuge in a morgue after a melting brain eater escapes containment. It has since stood on its own as a cult classic, generating its own sequels. This includes Brian Yuznaâs grotesque Return of the Living Dead 3, which I mostly bring up because it scared the shit out of me as a kid.

In 2024, Driscoll, who operates his own no-budget streaming service “DragonFLIX,” launched an Indiegogo page for “TRASH’s REVENGE Return of the Living Dead Universe.” Unlike other fan projects, this one had a large portion of the original cast involved, with stars Randolph and Linnea Quigley acting as producers. It also threw in Quigleyâs fellow Sorority Babe in the Slimeball Bowl-O-Rama Michelle Bauer and the Oscar nominated Eric Roberts, who has seemingly been in everything except The Living Dead.

From what Quigley described, this movie was intended to be a blend of Sunset Boulevard and Rocky Horror. Trash, Quigleyâs character who was last seen as a nudist zombie, had become a Norma Desmond recluse, relishing in the glory days of her brain eating spree. This sounds incredible. But after some confusion and radio silence between the cast and director, this incredible movie did not come to be.

Last Halloween night, Driscoll pushed out The Return of the Living Dead: Aftermath, an almost entirely AI generated heap of rotting flesh. The results wonât surprise you. Robotic line delivery. Nonsensical sequence of events. Object impermanence. Everythingâs wet. Everyone looks shocked. At one point the video just flips around like youâre watching on a phone someone dropped. And while the Return cast didnât film any of this footage, their likenesses are peppered throughout.

“It turned out to be a fiasco,” says Quigley. “I warned him, “Whatever you do, donât do any AI, because people donât like it, the fans donât like it.””

Living Dead alumni, even those who werenât attached to this film, have spoken out against Aftermath. They seem most concerned about the existing and continued use of their likeness, given that Driscoll has seemingly pivoted ‘Trashâs Revenge’ into an additional project. Randolph encourages those who provided any funding to ask for a refund through their credit card company. While Romeroâs original film was public domain, Return was not. Randolph also encourages Amazon, who bought MGM in 2022, to take legal action.

During Druski’s opening monologue, he said the powers that be at Saturday Night Live asked him to abide by two ground rules: no cussing and no whiteface. He said he couldn’t make either of those promises, and it’s a good thing he didn’t because the world needed to see his take on Elizabeth Holmes, which we got in a pre-tape that violated both of those ground rules.

The sketch in question is a stylistic take on the buzzy A24 documentary You Can See Everything and imagines an alternative world in which Holmes reaches out to Druski instead of Nathan Fielder. As you can imagine, Druski reacts a little differently than Fielder to many of the same moments from the movie, and we essentially get a highlight reel of his confused takes on things like her poor egg-making skills and the staring contest which he interprets as a sexual advance. Eventually, he even dresses up as Holmes herself and has a few wild exchanges. You can watch the madness below…

Druski, of course, is no stranger to whiteface. He went mega-viral earlier this year after he dressed up as a conservative white woman, who many felt was a version of Erika Kirk. The shortform sketches blew up everywhere and attracted both praise and some condemnation from the right wing. As such, it’s not exactly a shock to see Druski put the makeup on again, though I definitely didn’t see the Elizabeth Holmes angle coming.

Fortunately for fans of the comedian, he got plenty of opportunities to play other characters too. He gave us a political commentator, a Dominican phone salesman, a singer, a wedding photographer, an angry birthday girl and a corner guy who catcalls everyone walking past. Clearly, the writers wanted to give him a chance to show off his full range, and he was able to do that, both because he’s talented and because he jumped into every sketch without any hint of reservations or second guesses, which is what you need from a host.

Fans seemed really on board with what he was giving, and plenty of other celebrities were too. Druski’s episode gave us an early contender for what could be the most star-studded closing credits of the entire season. In addition to Emma Stone who appeared in his monologue, Walton Goggins who randomly performed with The Strokes and James Talarico who appeared in the cold open, we also got Dave Chappelle, Chris Rock, Michael B Jordan and Austin Butler who came out during Druski’s closing credits to support the comedian.

SNL fans should be in for a great episode next week too. Popular stand-up comedian and longtime writer on the show John Mulaney is returning to host again, which means we should get a bunch of over-the-top sketches and perhaps even a musical number. I can’t wait.

#3728. If You Loved 'Carrie,' There's One Movie You Need to Watch Next

Jeff Somers is a freelancer who has been writing about writing, books, personal finance, and home maintenance since 2012.

Jeff has published nine novels and more than 70 short stories; his story Ringing the Changes was selected for inclusion in The Best American Mystery Stories 2006. In 2018, Jeff published the book Writing Without Rules: How to Write & Sell a Novel Without Guidelines, Experts, or (Occasionally) Pants. He holds a bachelor’s degree in English and previously worked in medical publishing as a production editor.

When not writing, Jeff spends his free time fixing up his old house. He has tackled a wide range of DIY projects, including remodeling a bathroom entirely on his own in two weeks, and building a roof deck that hasn't fallen down yet. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Stephen King’s Carrie is one of those endlessly rebootable stories. Way back in 1974, King zeroed in on a near-perfect horror setup that explored being othered, the emotional and mental health consequences of bullying, and just how crappy being a teen girl can be in the modern world. Those themes—and the iconic visuals King conjured with his words—are evergreen, and resonate with audiences each time the story gets rebooted. Mike Flanagan has proved himself a master of horror and a clear successor to King’s legacy in the genre, and if you thought his Carrie reboot on Prime Video was terrific (and you’ve watched all the similar series out there), you should really watch Jennifer’s Body.

Carrie and Jennifer’s Body share a lot of themes—the corrosive pressure of high school, the casual cruelty of adolescents, the explosive power of feminine anger. While Jennifer Check (Megan Fox) is superficially presented as having more power and control than Carrie White (Summer H. Howell) because she’s more self-possessed (and played by Megan Fox), underneath the hair and makeup, Jennifer is just as naive and confused as Carrie. Both girls endure horrific experiences that set them on a path to horrific violence—and those experiences are symbolic of what women everywhere have to deal with all the damn time.

Just as in Carrie, Jennifer’s Body tracks a teen girl’s descent into monstrousness—but where Carrie leans into the tragic nature of those themes, Jennifer’s Body offers a funnier, more sarcastic take buoyed by Diablo Cody’s sharp dialogue and laugh-out-loud moments. The series highlights Carrie’s suffocating home life that offers her no relief from the grinding hell of being a 16-year-old girl who doesn’t quite fit the expected physical or behavioral norms imposed on teen girls, tracing a slow boil of rage. Jennifer’s Body depicts a character who ultimately chooses the dark path, leaning into her newfound destructive power, and has more fun with it, making it the perfect complement to the series.

Although the stories take different paths to get there, they both wind up at a cathartic and bloody climax centered on a school dance, where a lot of people die and chaos reigns. The film is the perfect way to examine, from a different angle, the themes that Carrie explores. Stream Jennifer’s Body on Hulu or rent it on Prime Video.

Looking for more stories about angry teen girls teaching society a terrifying lesson? Here are a few more films that make a perfect pairing with Carrie.

It’s been 50 years since Brian De Palma adapted King’s novel for the first time, and it’s still worth watching today, especially if you enjoyed Flanagan’s modern take. What could have been a trashy horror movie designed to cash in on the book’s success is instead a well-crafted film that makes every character feel real and consequential, and Sissy Spacek’s performance as Carrie is screen-meltingly amazing. Few horror films have aged this well, and watching a different creator’s vision of the story will be well worth your time. Rent Carrie on Prime Video.

If Carrie’s cathartic presentation of female rage and teen angst is what hooked you, the most relevant movie to jump to is The Craft. The story of four high school girls who harness dark powers to take revenge on, well, high school life itself is anchored by four feral performances from Robin Tunney, Fairuza Balk, Neve Campbell, and Rachel True. Like Jennifer’s Body, the teen protagonists enthusiastically embrace their power in a way that Carrie White doesn’t, but it transforms (and destroys them) just the same. Rent The Craft on Prime Video.

One reason Carrie is terrifying in all its forms? The very idea of a child with an imperfect grasp of ethics and an immature emotional state having thermonuclear-level psychic powers. After all, teenage girls without powers can be terrifying when triggered. The Innocents focuses on sisters Ida (Rakel Lenora Petersen Fløttum) and Anna (Alva Brynsmo Ramstad), who meet Ben (Sam Ashraf) and Aisha (Mina Yasmin Bremseth Asheim), who both demonstrate powers including telekinesis and mind control. Their interaction soon reveals that Anna also has mental powers, and the four begin working to enhance their capabilities—but when one of them begins using their powers to hurt others and seek revenge, things take a dark turn that fans of Carrie will appreciate. Stream The Innocents on Kanopy or rent it on Prime Video.

Anyone who was ever bullied in the teen years (so ... everyone) knows that those wounds never quite heal. That’s one aspect of Carrie’s power, and it’s also what makes Sissy an ideal movie to watch when you’ve finished the series. A mental health influencer, Cecilia (Aisha Dee)—once known as “Sissy”—runs into her old best friend, Emma (Hannah Barlow) and is unexpectedly invited to Emma’s bachelorette weekend—only to run into her childhood tormentor, Alex (Emily De Margheriti). The old trauma hits Cecilia like a bomb, shattering her fragile mental balance and leading to a surprisingly funny series of murders as Sissy works through her lingering anger issues. Stream Sissy on Hoopla or Tubi, or rent it on Prime Video.

If you’re a Mike Flanagan and Stephen King superfan, the obvious movie choice is their other collab, Doctor Sleep. A sequel to one of the most famous horror stories of all time (The Shining), the story finds a middle-aged Danny Torrance (Ewan McGregor) struggling to control his psychic powers, and leading the fight against an ancient group of entities that feed off of people like him. If you want more of that Flanagan/King magic, this is the right move. Rent Doctor Sleep on Prime Video.

Last Friday, the very good RPG Nier: Automata underwent what the scientific community calls 'puffer-fishification'. That is to say, it suddenly and inexplicably ballooned to over 700% of its original download size, as an update magically transformed the game from a reedy 50 GB lightweight into a 366-GB behemoth.

But it has since hit the Ozempic and is now back down to its regular size. "We have identified the cause and now resolved this issue," tweeted the official Nier X account earlier today. "Apologies for any inconvenience caused."

Notably absent from the bugfix notice was any explanation as to just what had happened. It might be academic at this point, but I for one would love to know how you accidentally make a game seven times bigger without anything changing.

Squenix is keeping schtum, but Rick Lane suggested, in our article last week about the bug, that it might have been related to Nier: Automata's DLC packages. "When selected for download on Steam, each DLC appears to have the same file size as the base game", he noted. "Weirdly though, this is only true for the initial download and installation. Once the game is installed, the file reportedly reverts to a more appropriate size of roughly 50 gigs." Indeed, the suggested temporary workaround for the issue (before Square Enix fixed it) was to uncheck all the DLCs when you installed the game.

So it sure seems like, somehow, the base files for the entire original game got attached to each individual DLC package. That might also explain why the size increase only applied to the downloads and not its install size—the whole game got downloaded eight times, but it was simply overwriting the base game files over and over.

That's just my speculation though, and without more news from Squenix, that's all we're gonna get. For now, enjoy being able to once again download 2B and 9S' adventures without having to start the download two weeks in advance.

#3725. Inside LA’s Election Night Parties as DSA-Backed Nithya Raman Threatens to Unseat Karen Bass

Ta-Nehisi Coates (Vanity Fair senior staff writer) recently said that if he reads “another scene from a DSA party in Brooklyn where people are drinking beer and doing whatever, I’m going to scream.”

But I can report that there were a lot of ecstatic and tipsy socialists in oversized vintage jackets at the DSA election party on the edge of Skid Row in Los Angeles Tuesday night. And, boy, did these socialists have a lot to celebrate.

Democrats were trouncing Republicans nationally. Democratic socialists were projected to take at least seven seats in the House, up from two. And in Los Angeles, the DSA’s preferred mayoral candidate, Nithya Raman, appeared poised to unseat Karen Bass. The incumbent Democratic mayor held a less than 1% lead in early returns, but ballots are expected to skew toward the more progressive candidate, Raman.

“Karen Bass said that she would need to be up 10 points on election night to be comfortable,” one DSA-LA leader told the crowd. He gestured at a graphic showing Bass’s narrow lead and said, “I’m not good at math because I’m gay. Is that 10 points? I don’t think so.” (Bass didn’t actually say that, but a pundit on KTLA did say something to that effect.)

Karen Bass during an election night event in Los Angeles, November 3, 2026.

At the DSA party, people cheered victories elsewhere in the country by socialists and establishment Democrats alike, but they booed when Bass appeared on television, and laughed when a Fox News commentator suggested the economy was doing well. At one point, organizers put on Hasan Piker’s livestream, and at another they played an AI-generated video showing Raman dancing while wearing a traditional Russian fur hat with ear flaps and a red star. When local TV station KTLA suggested Raman would likely win and Mayor Bass’s face appeared onscreen, someone shouted, “Whoa, get fucked, Karen.” It kind of encapsulated the strongest force animating the DSA members I talked to in this mayoral race: their dislike for Mayor Bass. They even called her the C-word onstage: “conservative.”

The DSA and Raman have had something of an on-again, off-again relationship. The organization helped propel her to an upset City Council victory in 2020, only to reprimand her over disagreements about Israel, housing policy, and the city’s mansion tax. The local DSA chapter endorsed her candidacy late in the campaign, but the national organization almost stripped it from her at the eleventh hour. The national DSA voted last week to preserve its Los Angeles chapter’s endorsement of Raman by a single vote, after a dispute over her refusal to embrace the movement to boycott Israel.

“I think people here have varying levels of begrudgingness about supporting Raman, but I think everyone here voted for her,” said one DSA-LA member at the party who worked on the chapter’s video team and declined to give her name.

Still, the DSA members at the party seemed to think this mayoral race offered another encouraging sign for their organization, even if Raman isn’t quite New York mayor Zohran Mamdani. She was attacked consistently by her opponents—mainly Spencer Pratt—as a dangerous extremist, but with the help of the DSA (it said members knocked on more than 110,000 doors this election cycle) she might be the first LA mayoral candidate to defeat an incumbent in over 20 years.

Meanwhile, at the Raman campaign’s official election night party at the Greek Theatre in Los Feliz, there weren’t any signs calling to “Tax the Rich” or to implement “Medicare for All,” as there were at the DSA party, but comedian Guy Branum from Apple TV’s Platonic sounded pretty similar to those socialists. He argued that Raman’s coalition reflected a class divide within Hollywood.

“Nithya has way more of entertainment’s middle class,” Branum said, describing workers worried about their next job. And Raman’s husband, television writer Vali Chandrasekaran, understands the industry’s problems firsthand, he argued.

Branum, who hangs with the couple socially, also wanted voters to appreciate one of her lessdiscussed qualifications. “They lead with the master’s in urban planning, and the Harvard, and the MIT,” he said. “But what you really need to see is that [she can dance]. You really need to see that hair let loose.” (Vanity Fair did not stick around at the party long enough to verify Raman’s dancing skills.)

Raman held her election night party at the Greek Theatre in Los Angeles, November 3, 2026.

Raman’s campaign manager, Ian Manheimer, was pretty psyched when he took the stage outside the Greek. “Holy shit! What is good, Los Angeles?” he shouted. Nearly three quarters of his campaign staff had never worked on a political campaign before, he told the crowd. Regardless, they managed to knock on over 100,000 doors, according to Manheimer.

The campaign’s grassroots operation had apparently become a bit of a competition. Volunteer Leo Blain, 25, told VF he’d knocked on more than 300 doors, putting him near the top of the campaign leaderboard. But the person to beat was Raman’s father, whom volunteers said had knocked on more than 1,000. All of that knocking was crucial, especially since Raman didn’t have a lot of institutional support or name recognition. Many of California’s most prominent Democrats stayed on the sidelines, because most of them would do anything to avoid the choice between an establishment incumbent and a rising DSA-endorsed challenger. But their neutrality didn’t necessarily mean indifference. A high-ranking official in Sacramento told me that plenty of state legislators were privately rooting for Bass, who had served as Speaker of the California Assembly before heading to Congress.

John, a DSA member who volunteered for Raman after having worked on Tom Steyer’s gubernatorial campaign, expected strong support for Raman among the local socialists, arguing that her independent thinking was a positive.

Raman’s party also included some unlikely converts. Kathleen Jensen, a Toluca Lake resident who previously supported Republican Rick Caruso, told me she considered Raman brilliant and wanted a “doer” in City Hall. Although she said some of her Democrat friends remained uneasy about Raman’s DSA association.

By 10:30 p.m., Bass’s election night party at the Loews Hotel in Hollywood had grown considerably quiet as her supporters began to digest the initial results. But the people who remained were still getting down to Snoop Dogg. The demographic differences between the parties were striking. Raman’s crowd skewed whiter, and more Asian, and the music was more alternative and disco. Bass’s crowd was notably more Black, reflecting the mayor’s decades of relationships in the city’s African American community.

Vaval Victor, 28, a member of Alpha Phi Alpha, the historically Black fraternity with which Bass has worked, remained confident that she would pull through. “She started the LA Black Dems Club in her kitchen,” he said, invoking her long history of organizing. “People are thirsty for hope.”

Bass had spent the campaign defending her record on homelessness, city finances, and last year’s catastrophic fires. Caruso, whom she defeated four years earlier, had swooped in at the end to say that he was voting for her, giving some of the city’s more conservative voters permission to support the incumbent. But early election-night returns were not the decisive advantage her campaign hoped for.

For all the divisions this mayoral race exposed, the three parties shared something that had been in short supply among Democrats lately: liberal joy.
