#3724. Google's 'Health Guardian' Is Now Available for Fitbits

Google’s “Health Guardian” feature set rolled out in late September to Pixel Watches 3, 4, and 5, and is now coming to Fitbit Air users in a new update. Google says the new features include reports on your blood pressure trends and on insulin resistance, which is a big claim for a wearable. Here’s what we know about Health Guardian, including how to set it up and what to expect.

Insulin resistance is associated with type 2 diabetes, and can be an early sign that you are heading toward pre-diabetes or diabetes. When your body’s insulin receptors stop responding as strongly to insulin, you’re more likely to have higher blood glucose.

Insulin resistance is normally measured with bloodwork. For example, your fasting glucose levels and fasting insulin are combined into a score called HOMA-IR. If you’re concerned about insulin resistance or pre-diabetes, it’s best to talk to an actual healthcare professional to find out what tests they recommend, and what to do with the results.

The insulin resistance feature coming to Google Health is, Google notes, “not intended for medical purposes” and “not a pre-screener for diabetes.”

Google published a paper describing some of the testing that went into developing its insulin resistance algorithm. In the study, the researchers had people use their own Fitbits or Pixel Watches to record a variety of metrics, including heart rate, HRV, and activity. It’s not clear from this paper exactly how the algorithm works or whether it’s likely to be useful in a general population, but apparently Google is betting on it being an interesting factor to track in your Google Health app.

Google also published a paper on a blood pressure algorithm, although it is not peer-reviewed. Instead of explaining how the algorithm works, it describes how the researchers tried to figure out what their AI-based model might be looking at. According to this paper, Google's model works about as well as clinical blood pressure measurements, but it's not clear how useful it would be in the real world. For example, the study excluded people with heart disease, but I'd imagine plenty of people with heart disease would be interested in their blood pressure scores.

Google said last month in a press release that Health Guardian, which includes insulin resistance and blood pressure trends, is available for free for people who use a Pixel Watch 3, 4, or 5. Fitbit Air users, they added, would get blood pressure and insulin resistance trends “with a Google Health Premium subscription later this year.” "Later" has arrived, as the feature for Fitbit users is in Google Health 5.11, available on both Android and iOS.

So it’s free if you have a Pixel Watch, but not if you only have the Fitbit Air: Google Health Premium is $9.99/month. It’s unclear what happens if you own both devices; presumably, having a Pixel Watch will get you free access. In any case, other devices, including older Fitbits, do not seem to be included.

The Pixel Watch got Health Guardian in the 5.09 release of the Google Health app for Android. The Fitbit got Health Guardian in the 5.11 release for both Android and iOS.

You can set up your blood pressure and insulin resistance tracking as soon as you get the new version of the Google Health app. I was able to set up insulin tracking by going to the health tab and then tapping Metabolic, and I set up blood pressure under Heart. If you go to Respiratory, you can also set up sleep-breathing quality. (Some European users will get a feature that can call for help in a "breathing emergency," but that is not available in the U.S.)

Google said that the insulin and blood pressure features will give you a monthly report on the first of each month, with the first report coming Oct. 1, if you have given the watch enough data in the previous month. If you're a Fitbit user and are just setting up the feature now, you'll get your first report on Nov. 1. Here is what the app requires:

For blood pressure reports: You need to wear the watch for five consecutive days in the previous month (so, in October to get your November report). You don't have to wear the watch at night.

For insulin resistance: You need to wear the watch for seven days and nights in the previous month, but they don't need to be consecutive.

I set up both features as soon as I got the update for the Pixel Watch, but that timeline didn't allow me a full seven days and nights before the October report. That means I don't have an insulin resistance result. I do have my blood pressure trend result: "Not High." As a reminder, a watch cannot know your actual blood pressure, so the watch is making estimates based on data that may not correspond with your actual blood pressure. That said, my blood pressure tends to read in the normal range at doctors' visits, so at least this wasn't surprising.

What's more confusing is what you're actually supposed to do about the results. If your watch says your blood pressure or insulin are fine, would you delay seeking care or abandon a treatment or lifestyle change that was supposed to help you? If your watch says something is wrong, would you believe that and maybe spend unnecessary time and money getting checked out? Pixel Watch users are discussing their results online, with a variety of reactions. One redditor says: "I awoke to find out that my blood pressure is too high and apparently the insulin in my body does nothing. This despite that my most recent doctor's visit and blood work were all perfectly normal." Another said: "I got this high insulin result this morning. I have really changed my diet the last four months and I have been going to the gym regularly. I have lost about 40 pounds this year. It's a bummer to see this. I just wonder if it's accurate." I wonder that, too.

#3723. Super Smash Bros. Creator Masahiro Sakurai Cautions Against The Use Of Gen AI: ‘We Can Come Up With Better Ideas’

During an event celebrating 40 years of Japanese game magazine Famitsu, Super Smash Bros. supremo Masahiro Sakurai participated in a talk where he discussed his career and work. He shared his thoughts about generative AI, confirming that he has not yet used the technology for any of his current projects, and remains cautious over how useful the tool is in its current state.

The talk was held to coincide with the release of a new book in Japan compiling Sakuraiâs writings for Famitsu magazine. Over the course of the 18 years between 2003 and 2021, Sakurai wrote a column for Famitsu discussing the ever-evolving state of games development and his experience managing the shifting expectations and technologies within the industry. Alongside discussing his past work, the famed game director took some time to address many of the modern concerns facing the industry, including the growing debate surrounding generative AI. At least for now, Sakurai doesn’t think AI can handle tasks in games development or even the brainstorming process, and believes that âwe can come up with better ideas by thinking about them for ourselves.â

âThereâs more [to game development] than simply coming up with an idea,â Sakurai explained. âItâs not enough to just think up an idea. Lots of different factors come into consideration here, like whether you have a fixed deadline or if your team can do it, does it fit into your budget, and so on.â

Currently, Sakurai also believes the technology is not strong enough to even be used for brainstorming ideas, due to the need to factor in the realities of development and the limits on the sort of results it can come up with. He hasnât used it in any of his recent games, including the most recent Kirby Air Raiders, and currently has no plans to use it, doubtful of its capabilities.

That being said, he doesnât rule out its use entirely, as a result of the demands of players and the industry putting increased strain on the development pipeline. According to him, work on Kirby Air Riders was ten times more demanding than it was on the GameCube original, and he notes that there are examples of games unable to turn a profit even after selling millions of units. In order to bring down costs and make these games viable, he suggests the use of AI may be necessary in the future when the technology improves.

âIf you remain stuck on the idea of not using AI because itâs not trustworthy enough as a technology, thereâs a risk that you may fall further and further behind,â Sakurai ponders. âCompared to developers who make games without it, I believe those using AI without hesitation are likely to be able to create more games. As a result, not using may also be a bad idea.â

Developers from Shigeru Miyamoto to Kotaro Uchikoshi have shared varied opinions on the future use cases for AI within the Japanese games industry, and the broad adoption or regulation of AI by Japanese studios. As seen with developers like Sakurai, however, not all are willing to embrace the technology, or feel that generative AI is ready to be trusted with major development tasks.

I never get tired of seeing celebrities throw on stunning outfits and pose in front of the beloved “Urban Light” lampost exhibition at the LACMA. This year we got memorable looks from the likes of Kylie Jenner, Nicole Kidman and more. Everyone really dressed out for the LACMA Art + Film Gala this year, but it’s Emily Ratajkowski’s gravity-defying dress I’m still thinking about.

I mean how could I not be? Long gowns usually only come in so many silhouettes, but every now and again a celebrity tries something I’ve never seen before. The curiosity factor was really present in Ratajkowski’s long, flowy dress at the 2026 event not just because it was pretty, but because I couldn’t figure out how the author, model and social media star was avoiding a wardrobe malfunction.

A post shared by Emily Ratajkowski (@emrata)

Hear me out. This dress is gorgeous. It hugs in just the right places, but it’s also made from a completely unstructured material and it does not seem to have a real strap on the left side. I wondered if the large metal pendant on the Gucci dress was just weighted and holding up the left side of the dress with nothing else for support, but that feels brazen. Given the dress is also backless, it’s not simply a cleverly-constructed one-shoulder dress. It’s all very confusing.

It’s also barely connected at the hip before a dramatic slit draws one’s eye. Honestly, like Kim Kardashian’s “not for you to understand” dress and other celebrity fashion looks before her, I’m not sure how the Gucci look works. This isn't the first time Ratjkowski's flipped the fashion script on a red carpet, either. Regardless, this dress is unlike any other dress I’ve seen, and it’s definitely worth talking about.

Meanwhile, no one was really a slouch at the LACMA event. Nicole Kidman gave off elegant ballet vibes with her own frock. Her dress was unsurprisingly Chanel, as Kidman had just appeared at a Chanel Cruise Show fashion event alongside Margot Robbie earlier this week.

A post shared by Nicole Kidman (@nicolekidman)

And Kylie Jenner literally sparkled under the lamppost lights of the LACMA. Her Ashi Studio Gown was pretty up front, but it was the back of the dress that really shone. (Kylie loves a good backless dress, so no surprise there.)

Ultimately, there were many different celebrity takes at the LACMA event, and I was here for a lot of them, but it's this Gucci dress I'm still going to be puzzling out this week.

#3721. My Favorite Travel Headphones Are $250 Off Right Now

As a headphone reviewer, not many headphones outside of the flagship Sony, Bose, and Apple models get me excited. However, the JBL Tour One M3 Smart Tx headphones became the exception to that rule when I started using them over my Sony 1000XM6 as my go-to headphones. And right now, the Tour One M3s are down to $199.95 (originally $449.95), their lowest price ever, according to price-tracking tools. This is a great deal for these headphones, which I deemed my favorite travel headphones in my review.

Everything from design to the features on the Tour One M3 was made with travel in mind. The headphones are very light, which, along with the comfortable soft earcups and headband, makes them great for wearing for long periods of time. I was able to wear these on a long flight without feeling any discomfort. Feeling like you're not wearing any headphones is the gold standard for comfort, and the Tour One M3 nails that aspect. The battery life is also impressive, with up to 70 hours with ANC off and 40 hours with it on.

The travel case is compact, convenient, and has extra storage for the audio transmitter, which is the best feature of the Tour One M3. This is a high-quality, low-latency audio transmitter. Anything that you can plug an AUX cable, USB, or USB-C port into can stream high-quality, 24-bit audio wirelessly to the Tour One M3. The main way most people will use these headphones is by plugging them into the in-flight entertainment, which lets you watch movies in high-quality LDAC with ANC. But I've also been able to use them to watch TV.

The Tour One M3 Smart Tx are incredible traveling headphones, especially at $199.95, and I recommend them to anyone who values comfort, battery life, simplicity, and likes the idea of the audio transmitter.

#3720. Tim Burton Partners With Loewe for a ‘Nightmare Before Christmas’ Capsule Collection

“Things in life are the best as surprises,” says Tim Burton, the iconoclast filmmaker, calling from London. More than 40 years after making his directorial debut with Pee-wee’s Big Adventure (1985), and penning the poem that would eventually inspire The Nightmare Before Christmas, Burton is expanding his artistic remit once more. The director has partnered with Jack McCollough and Lazaro Hernandez, the designers of Loewe, for a new capsule collection featuring memorable vignettes and characters from the latter film. “When they came to me and were talking about it,” Burton tells Vanity Fair, “I just got very excited, because I’m a frustrated designer myself.”

The capsule, available starting November 12, includes a range of handbags with whimsical recreations of the film’s most beloved characters. Zero, Jack Skellington’s dog, floats on the side of a handbag; the Harlequin Demon is rendered with feathers and leather scales; and Skellington himself is painted as a peekaboo surprise inside a carryall.

“They took something that means a lot to me and they put their own spin on it,” he says of working with Loewe. “The way they make things, the textures and the elements involved are just beautiful,” he continues. “It’s exciting for me to see it happen.”

Jack Skellington peekaboos from the inside of a handbag.

Snakes pop out of a woven leather bucket bag.

In the more than three decades since the film was released, Jack Skellington and The Nightmare Before Christmas have become synonymous with a certain brand of Halloween-like spookiness, a soft spot for Christmas and the holidays, and a wondrous gothic style and sensibility. The film originated from a poem Burton wrote in 1982 while working as an animator at Walt Disney Productions. “It was something that came not so much from a thought, but was just more slightly from the subconscious,” Burton says in a documentary short accompanying the Loewe collection.

But just as film and animation have changed over the years, the meaning of the film and its legacy have too. The Nightmare Before Christmas has become arguably one of the most renowned stop-motion-animation films. The painstaking process of making the film required the creation of 227 puppets and the shooting of 109,440 frames to bring the story to life. “I love [stop motion] because it’s all handmade,” Burton says. “When you see the puppets and the sets, you wish everybody could experience the tactile nature of what goes into making a stop-motion film, or any film.”

In the age of artificial intelligence, the movie has become a symbol of human craft and ingenuity. “The more it keeps going that way,” Burton says of the proliferation of AI, “the more I appreciate [the human] side of it. I think it’s something that’s very important to keep in the world, the tactile, not being on a screen all the time and doing all that sort of thing. To me, [humanity] is very important to life and art and anything, really.”

A still from a documentary short featuring Burton that accompanies the collection.

Rather than be overly protective about some of his most famous intellectual property, Burton wanted to let the legacy leather-goods house and its designers follow their own instincts. “They consulted me, and we talked about this and that, but I respect them and I respect what they do,” he says. “It’s more fun for me to see things beautifully done.” Fashion, after all, he says, is a medium different from film. “I mean, I’ve seen Nightmare merchandise, and some of it’s good and some of it’s really bad,” he says with a laugh. “And even the bad ones are kind of good sometimes.” One example? A “big fat Jack Skellington.” “Well, no, he’s not a big fat Jack Skellington, but as a stuffed little toy, he’s kind of cute,” Burton adds with a laugh. “Things change and mutate, and you just [need to] keep the spirit of something, but then do something [with] your own interpretation of it.”

Many members of The Nightmare Before Christmas’s original 1993 audience are now adults atop creative industries. Burton’s work, in a way, is part of their own imagination. “The things that inspired you from the very beginning, they just stay with you,” Burton says. “Whether it’s conscious or not, it’s just part of your DNA.”

Revisiting past work, Burton says, “can be a beautiful experience, but not always.” Though he says he “had no real desire” to make a sequel to Nightmare, Burton did direct 2024’s Beetlejuice Beetlejuice, a sequel to the 1988 film Beetlejuice, starring Winona Ryder and Catherine O’Hara. Returning to the film 35 years later “made sense” for him “emotionally.” “It was like, nobody’s getting any younger and blah, blah, blah,” Burton says. “I really did that movie not to make a sequel, but it was something that I enjoyed, and we tried to do it in the style of the first movie, shot it quickly, did live effects. So it was an experience that meant a lot to me. And I think for me, it’s always important to make something that I really, really feel.”

Burton illustrating some of his characters.

There’s plenty of interest in Burton revisiting other parts of his oeuvre too. Since the release of Corpse Bride in 2005, fans have been clamoring for a live-action remake of the film. Burton laughs when asked if he’d ever honor the request, and while he doesn’t deliver a straight answer, he doesn’t exactly say no. “I’ve got thoughts swirling around and all sorts of things going on, but I’ve been through too much to go, Okay,” he says, noting that he’s had projects mutate and change over the years. “I keep it open, and I’m just finishing something, so I’m in an open spot now, and I’m really excited to look for what the next thing is.”

Away from the big screen, Burton has experienced somewhat of a resurgence with the success of Netflix’s Wednesday, and he’s enjoyed ventures outside of the film industry. This capsule with Loewe is one of those projects, and the director also collaborated with A$AP Rocky, whom he describes as “a real artist,” for the visual rollout of his album released earlier this year, Don’t Be Dumb, creating characters for its cover and a music video. “I love this stuff because film has [become] such a business. It’s gotten so big,” he says. “That’s why I enjoyed doing stuff with Rocky. It’s what I love doing, and it’s just a different form of doing it.”

Burton hasn’t been on the lookout for new opportunities, but he likes being surprised by them. “It’s always just this nice, beautiful, strange surprise when somebody asks to do something or collaborate,” he says. “I mean, that’s what film’s all about. You’re working with different artists and you’re working with different people with one [goal] in mind. So it’s not that much different. I like those kinds of surprises.”

#3719. Sony Announces New Japan-Only PlayStation Portal With Internal Storage

Sony have announced a new Japan-only version of the Playstation Portal, with all-new functionality in the form of internal storage exclusive to the domestic edition of the device.

Last November, Sony released a Japan-only region-locked and language-locked edition of the PS5, reducing the price of this digital-only model from 73,000 ($461) to 55,000 yen ($347). In recent generations, thanks to the success of the Nintendo Switch in Japan and the high cost of PlayStation platforms compared to wages and the cost of living, Sonyâs once-dominant position has diminished. Sony’s Japan-only PS5 aped the decision by Nintendo to create a cheaper, region-specific Nintendo Switch 2. Now Sony is repeating this tactic for the new Japan-only PlayStation Portal, but this time the device appears to be an upgraded version of the hardware.

Although this new PlayStation Portal boasts the same 1080p LCD screen and general features as the worldwide iteration of the device, for this latest version Sony has added internal storage as an all-new feature. Oddly, however, it wonât yet say what it plans to do with this storage. Sony has only said that it “will confirm the future functionality at a later date.” Due to the addition of internal storage, the price of this Japan-only model will be identical to the global model at 39,980 yen ($252), and will be sold in Midnight Black, the same color variant as the Japan-only PS5.

The regular PlayStation Portal can only stream games, either directly from a PlayStation console or via the cloud. The lack of storage prevents games from being downloaded to the device, even though it has its own mobile chipset that, while different to PS5’s, would in theory be capable of running some games locally.

Does this new storage option mean that Sony will enable support for select titles to run natively? Will a similar device with internal storage also be sold internationally? Sony has yet to confirm anything at this time, but considering the success of Portal and the rumors of a next-generation portable, this certainly lends credence to the possibility of a hybrid approach. Pre-orders for the new Japan-only PlayStation Portal begin on Thursday, with a release date planned for December 10.

I've spent far too much of my life covering the rampant ascent of AI. A juggernaut of tech development, destined to change the world into some sort of sci-fi utopia (if you believe its advocates) or fated to come crashing down around our ears, taking a large chunk of the world economy with it. Or the end of the world as we know it, according to some.

And now, the pillars upon which the AI revolution sits seem to be shaking beneath it. The most recent tremors began with the wobbling of US AI-led tech stocks in mid-October, after a similar descent in China earlier this year. Then at the end of the month, while many tech companies reported huge amounts of revenue in their quarterly financial results, some AI tech share prices still slid under a black cloud of investor doubt.

None more so than Alphabet, the owner of Google. A $500 billion wipe in stock price, led by the admission that the company's own AI search features were eating into its ad revenue, rocked the market. A wider tech sell-off, fuelled by fears regarding the eventual profitability of AI and a potential upcoming Democrat victory in the US midterms, rattled the valuations of many AI tech companies—alongside the chip manufacturers sitting underneath them.

All this, of course, amid a backdrop of increasing AI-related concerns across multiple fields. Rogue AI agents. Increasing AI-powered cybersecurity incidents. Predictions of the end of civilisation, brought on by rampant AI development without proper oversight. Fears of job market ruination. AI psychosis. The list goes on.

Then, the so-called blue wave came to pass. Democrats won control of both the US House and the Senate. Such sweeping political changes can rarely be ascribed to a single factor, but US voter polling indicates that data center expansion was a key source of voter frustration. The current Republican administration has gone all in on AI, and much of the US public seems displeased at the idea of massive AI tech facilities springing up left, right, and center across the country.

Jensen Huang has hit the headlines over allegations surrounding his involvement with an alleged Chinese spy.

Trillions were wiped off US tech stock values as investors sold off increasing numbers of shares in tech companies, amid further fears that the great AI infrastructure buildout was about to be reigned in by political changes. Long-called-for regulation of AI and AI companies seemed—and indeed, still seems—ever more likely.

And now, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has hit the headlines over allegations surrounding his involvement with an alleged Chinese spy. At first, it was reported that Alice Huang (no relation) had a "close relationship" with the Nvidia chief.

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

Now, Jensen Huang has himself admitted that the two were engaged in an affair, and Nvidia has launched an internal investigation into concerns related to national security. The timing could not be worse for the US tech market. At the time of writing, Nvidia's share value has sunk in pre-market trading.

The company is, in many ways, the backbone of the AI revolution, the chief provider of the chips behind the sweeping AI rollout that has changed the tech landscape over the past few years, and the creator of the CUDA platform that underpins it. Huang is its charismatic leader, the relentless optimist behind this AI-led future we're supposedly about to enjoy. A scandal at this stage is likely the last thing any tech investor wants to see.

So, what now? While the long-mooted AI bubble burst has yet to materialise in full, it's certainly looking like the relentless "all the money in the world" optimism phase is coming to an end. Investors are shaken, with worries about long-term profitability continuing to eat into the market, alongside US national security concerns now dominating the headlines.

The train with no brakes is rocking wildly against the tracks—and unfortunately, given AI and big tech's role in the global economy, we're all stuck in the carriages behind it.

The relentless "all the money in the world" optimism phase is coming to an end.

I'm no economist. I can't tell you if this is the beginning of the AI bubble pop, or whether this is merely an extremely turbulent time in the AI success story. Certainly, it seems like the horse has already bolted, and that AI is here to stay in some form or fashion. Those hoping for a return to the good old, pre-AI days are almost certain to be disappointed.

But, having reported on so many "AI doomsayers" over the past few years, I can tell you that a fall from grace has been predicted by many. Such a massive, world-changing technological development, fuelled by seemingly impossible amounts of investment, has always seemed destined to face some sort of financial reckoning.

That reckoning, I believe, has never looked closer. May you live in interesting times, as the old saying goes. And what happens next? Well, it's going to be interesting, at the very least.

Justin Timberlake has produced more than a few hit songs as a solo artist over the course of his illustrious career, and one that continues to penetrate the zeitgeist is 2006’s “What Goes Around... Comes Around”. The hit song has in some ways become something of a breakup anthem and, as a result, one rumor has been swirling around it for years. Many have speculated that the song is inspired by Timberlake’s split from Britney Spears. Now, Timberlake himself is clearing the air and explaining the real backstory.

As of late, Timberlake has been somewhat nostalgic, as he’s been looking back on his musical creations. The Grammy Award winner recently sat down with Complex for an interview (which is on YouTube) and ranked his best songs. While discussing “What Goes Around…”, Timberlake said that he felt compelled to address the long-standing rumor related to the tune. Apparently, the song is not about him but about another person’s experience, and he went on to explain how everything came together:

Maybe I should dispel a rumor at this point, which has gone around forever, which is like it's not a personal story from mine. It's actually a personal story from a friend that I asked permission to [use as] inspiration. Funny enough, I asked. I was like — he was just going through it. And he was telling me what had happened, and I said, ‘Do you mind if I write about this?’ And I quote, my friend said, ‘Yeah, torch that bitch. What goes around comes around.’

Now, if that last comment couldn’t be viewed as a sign, then I don’t know what could’ve. This is definitely an intriguing piece of lore on one of JT’s signature songs. What’s more is that while Timberlake has talked about the challenges of writing hit songs, his experience penning “What Goes Around…” sounds like a walk in the park:

I was like, ‘I have to go. Thank you. I have to go. I have to go.’ He's like, ‘What?’ I was like, ‘I got it. I got it.’ And I hung up the phone. And so I had the idea. I just went in and, again, this song was written in, I mean, damn near 20 minutes…. It was just flowing. The interlude that goes with it, like it's just — and then you put the video with it. There's a 10-minute video we shot for it. This just hit on all cylinders for me.

It was in 1999 that Justin Timberlake began dating Britney Spears, who he had previously worked with on The All-New Mickey Mouse Club. The pair became an it-couple during the early aughts, and the relationship eventually ended on a sour note in 2002. At that time, Timberlake allegedly sent Spears a breakup text message that she received while filming the “Overprotected: The Darkchild Remix” music video. In the aftermath, Timberlake released the hit 2002 track, “Cry Me A River” and, in 2011, he confirmed the Spears split inspired it.

Much has been said and written about the Spears/Timberlake relationship, and it has remained a topic of discussion. Spears herself even discussed aspects of the relationship in her best-selling 2023 memoir, The Woman in Me. In that book, Spears covered more than a few topics, including the abortion she had in 2000, which she said came after Timbelake told her he “didn’t want to be a father” at the time. While Timberlake has been honest about not saying sorry to “nobody,” he was allegedly concerned ahead of the book’s release.

Of course, at this point, both Justin Timberlake and Britney Spears are in different places in their lives. The pair don’t seem to be in regular contact, though Timberlake did apologize to Spears in 2021 for his role in the personal setbacks she experienced and expressed support ahead of her conservatorship ending. I don’t see the two getting back on regular speaking terms again. Still, at least the “What Goes Around... Comes Around” rumor is now cleared up.

#3714. Elon Musk Spent $474 Million on the 2026 Midterm Elections. On Election Day, He Fell Silent.

Elon Musk, the Tesla CEO and former intimate of President Donald Trump’s, may have ever so slightly eroded his 14 (that we know of) children’s inheritances during the 2026 midterm elections, spending $474 million (of his estimated $901.7 billion bankroll) on Republican campaigns across the US. But as Election Day continued across the country, the prolific user of his own social media platform, X, remained relatively restrained.

“Vote red today,” was an early tweet, interspersed between abundant promotions of his company’s AI agent, Grok Bot. A shared tweet featuring Michigan Democratic US Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed was simply captioned with the raised eyebrow emoji.

And that was the most Musk had to say about the midterms on Tuesday, despite what The New York Times reports is the most that “any donor has ever spent in a single election cycle,” barring former New York City mayor Michael R. Bloomberg’s spend on his own 2020 presidential campaign, which cost him more than $1 billion.

And as the blue wave continued, Musk started removing tweets instead of adding them. Early Wednesday morning, around the time James Talarico took the stage to celebrate his win in Texas, Musk removed the missive he had pinned to the top of his account, an October 29 post in which he said his “biggest concern…if there is a clean sweep by Democrats of the House, Senate and Presidency in 2028,” is that they will open the borders, create a larger Supreme Court, and grant statehood to DC and Puerto Rico. “That is why you should vote for Republican senators this election,” he concluded. "Other reasons are irrelevant compared to this one.”

Per the Times, Musk’s spend is likely to exceed the $474 million currently reported, as any donations made after October 14 have yet to be counted. Of that current figure, $216 million went to his own super PAC (America PAC), with $212 of that going to support US Senate hopeful Ken Paxton. An additional $168 million went to the pro-Republican Senate Leadership Fund, and $30 million went to the Congressional Leadership Fund, the primary super PAC for House Republicans. An additional $16 million went to state-focused political efforts in Michigan, Texas, and Wisconsin, while $44 million went to federal Republican groups or candidates.

That’s a lot of money to most of us, but by early Wednesday morning, Musk appeared to be taking the expenditure in stride. “Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now,” he tweeted at 1:12 a.m. ET, followed almost immediately by “Guess my election-interfering space lasers didn’t work this time,” punctuated by the shrug emoji.

“I think we have enough power in the machine,” the former chairman of SIE Worldwide Studios told The Trophy Room in a recent interview. “The innovation needs to come not from making PS6 for $1,200âit’s to make another PS5 for $300. Now, that would be true innovation.”

Layden has been a critic of the console war arms race in recent years, arguing that improvements have become increasingly hard to spot with the naked eye while sitting in anything less than pristine viewing conditions. “I mean, the the jump from PS1 to PS2 was incredible, right?” he said. “And the jump from compact disc to DVD, different storage medium, higher density, and then from two to three when you got to 1080p and you can really do 60 frames per second at uh, you know, at a high frame rate. #3711. Of Mics and Men: After MAGA Meltdown, the Manosphere Winds Down

Two years ago, on the night of the 2024 presidential election, Ultimate Fighting Championship CEO Dana White took to the podium at Donald Trump’s Palm Beach victory party and rattled off a list of thank-yous to some rowdy podcasters and YouTube pranksters: the NELK Boys, Adin Ross, Theo Von, Bussin’ With the Boys, and “last but not least, the mighty and powerful Joe Rogan.” Just months before, these names were seldom mentioned in the mainstream press, but now they were recognized on a national stage as having powered Trump’s return to office by hosting him on their platforms and revealing his more personable side. The victory that night seemed to go well beyond the electoral conquest; one of the defining cultural legacies of the 2024 election cycle is the imprecise but vivid concept of the manosphere.

By 2026, the novelty of Trump and Von joking about the potency of cocaine, as they did in one of the signature moments of the 2024 campaign, has worn off. The president’s approval rankings tanked despite his enduring presence as a pop culture figure. Rogan endorsed Trump in the final days of that 2024 race, but he recently described Trump’s “really crazy” 1,300-word Truth Social tirade against Bill Maher as having the ring of a “girl who got dumped.” He has roundly criticized Trump’s handling of the Epstein Files, a signature issue for the podcast class, and described the Iran war as a “betrayal.” If the end of MAGA is in sight amid Tuesday’s blue tsunami, so is the notion that Republicans had captured the coveted, low-propensity demographic of young men: The New York Times estimated that Democrats won 18-to-29-year-old men by 24 points on Tuesday, a 38-point swing from Trump’s 2024 victory among them. Democrats are content creators too now, and the most notable political appearance on The Joe Rogan Experience over the past couple of years was James Talarico’s. “You need to run for president,” Rogan told Texas’s new senator-elect.

And so when C-SPAN made the somewhat mind-boggling announcement that the staid public-affairs network would simulcast election night coverage hosted by Patrick Bet-David, a Florida-based podcaster known for his interviews with Andrew Tate and Nick Fuentes, it was less of a capitulation to the so-called manosphere than an emblem of the modern media free-for-all. Of the online personalities loosely associated with Rogan’s milieu, Bet-David’s backstory is the most colorful. A refugee from Iran, he joined the Army upon arriving in the United States; he has said he worked for a time as a bodyguard to a high-level Los Angeles cocaine dealer. Bet-David now operates a media company called Valuetainment, formed after he made his riches with an insurance company that has been widely described as a multi-level marketing operation. After interviewing the leading looksmaxxing personality, Clavicular, last week, he was now responsible for providing C-SPAN’s conservative perspective. A spokesperson for the network described the programming to me as an effort to achieve “a marriage of traditional media and new media.”

“In the 2024 election, we invited Pete Buttigieg, God knows how many times, never showed up,” Bet-David told me in the lead-up to the evening. “Pete Buttigieg was here last week. We did a two-hour podcast together right before the midterms. And so the market is realizing that’s the direction you got to go.”

As he entertained a characteristically ragtag group of political-for-the-night personalities, Bet-David sat at his decision desk in a pinstripe suit with cartoonishly wide peak lapels. There were the young conservative provocateurs CJ Pearson and Nick Shirley, and the Groyper-adjacent, recent Florida gubernatorial candidate James Fishback, who described the night as a “really tough election for my party.”

Bet-David joked to Michael Franzese that he knows about gas prices—before refashioning himself as a political commentator, the former Colombo crime family capo ran a multi-million-dollar gasoline tax bootlegging scheme in the 1980s. In voicing his opposition to the war in Iran, Franzese said, “We had a saying on the street, the best way to defeat your enemies is to make them your friends.” He bemoaned how Trump “makes everything all about him.”

Other guests included Ann Coulter, Piers Morgan, Roger Stone, Bill O’Reilly, and Cenk Uygur, whose Young Turks show was simulcasting on another C-SPAN channel. For some reason, Jackass’s Steve-O appeared toward the end of the night. He pointed out to Bet-David that Marco Rubio is “stronger for you guys” than JD Vance.

Two years ago, I watched a similar scene unfold in an airplane hangar in Fort Lauderdale. It was, as Bet-David and I agreed on Tuesday, a wild night: He was hosting an election night party at Valuetainment’s headquarters at the peak of the manosphere chatter and at the onset of what seemed to so many to be the era of MAGA cultural domination. Men in tightly tapered polyester pants hopped out of Ferraris and Teslas to watch a crowd of UFC fighters, rappers, former mobsters, and Candace Owens wax poetic about how the age of Jennifer Lopez and Beyoncé, who had appeared alongside Kamala Harris in previous weeks, was over. In this new era of masculinity, there was no time anymore for liberal Hollywood political pieties: Mark Zuckerberg had just started wearing a gold chain and describing Trump’s fist pump after the attempted assassination as “one of the most badass things I’ve ever seen in my life.”

And the vibe shift, as it could only be called, was shocking for a period. There was a moment, for instance, in the heady aftermath of the 2024 election when Von attended an Oscars week poker night hosted by Timothée Chalamet at the Chateau Marmont. (The actor had recently appeared on his show.) Just weeks later, Von was at a UFC fight where White warmly embraced the Tate brothers. The entire category of celebrity appeared to be flattening in real time.

But to those on the inside of the podcaster-comedian boom, another swing of the pendulum already seemed to be coming. Andrew Schulz, a frequent Rogan guest, conducted one of Trump’s trademark podcast interviews in the summer of 2024. “After the Trump thing, I wasn’t like, ‘We got it now,’” he told me the following year. “After the Trump thing, I was like, ‘We just interviewed the president of the United States, what the fuck?’” He thought that the deafening manosphere discourse might indicate the presence of a cultural bubble. “I just think that we are what people are listening to now,” he said, “but that could change tomorrow.”

Alex Bruesewitz, a 29-year-old Trump adviser, was largely credited with orchestrating the candidate’s podcast tour in 2024. A social media operative who had built connections with big-name celebrities, influencers, and podcasters in the lead-up to the presidential election—he brokered Trump’s alliance with Nicki Minaj and recently flew on Air Force One with Mike Tyson—Bruesewitz told me on Wednesday morning that he had soured on the Republican party.

“I consider myself more of a Trump voter than a Republican voter,” he said. “If the party moves in the direction of people like Ted Cruz, for example, in 2028, there’s going to be a lot of people like myself…who will not participate in the Republican elections moving forward.”

In the midterms cycle, Bruesewitz said, the podcasting world “wasn’t there for us to engage.” The likes of Von and Schulz have echoed Rogan’s criticisms of the Iran war and how the Trump administration managed the release of the Epstein files.

“I don’t think that any of them were ever team Trump,” he said. “We simply just had conversations with them in 2024. The post-election reaction, saying that they’re part of this right-wing manosphere, I think that actually had an effect on how they covered us during our first two years. I think that they didn’t want to be labeled right-wing, and so they evened out a bit.”

Another reason, Bruesewitz supposed, for the end of Republican podcasting dominance and the blue tsunami: “Republican candidates were really lame and they weren’t interesting people…there was a little bit of an expectation that these candidates could go communicate with low-propensity voters with podcasting again, but I pushed back on their teams. I was like, Look, there’s zero percent chance that any of these podcasters are going to want to have on your boring candidates.”

By the end of the night on Tuesday, Bet-David and Steve-O were making plans to hang out before the stuntman left town. All of the guests on the C-SPAN–Bet-David collaboration seemed likely to keep talking about politics online, but it would be difficult to assign any of them a specific party agenda. In the airplane hangar two years prior, Bet-David had ended the night with what felt like a seismic exhortation, telling a raucous crowd, “For the rest of our lives we will share this night together.” On Tuesday, he was more practical as he signed off for the evening.

#3710. I’ve Played Zelda: Ocarina Of Time Way Too Much To Enjoy The Remake As Much As It Deserves

Game DiaryRemakeSwitch 2The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina Of Time

I’m not sure exactly how many times I’ve played The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, but it’s a lot. Back in the days of the Nintendo 64, we weren’t drowning in new releases or free-to-play forever games. You played what you had. And if what you had was good, you played it again and again.

Ocarina of Time was very good and I probably played it a couple of times a year. The remake is gorgeous. It’s also more faithful than I was expecting. I’ve gone through these motions before. Never like this, but enough to not feel as impressed as I should be.

I’m currently making my way through the Gerudo Fortress. My kids and I took turns throughout most of the weekend (I may have had a habit of passing the controller every time we had to go back to the Temple of Time, transform back into Young Link, and run back across Hyrule Field to unlock the next step in a quest). I’ve shown them the original game, but they still feel like this is something completely different. I wish I could feel the same.

I don’t remember every secret in the game and I was never much of a completionist. I would be useless trying to unlock the Biggoron Sword without a guide. But all of the beats along the critical path remain surprisingly familiar, pushed to the forefront of my mind as I encounter each one in the remake. The many ways in which the new version has been streamlined have only served to further that feeling of going back through the motions. The tightly orchestrated logic of the puzzles also reinforces that.

These motions should not be underestimated. The controls are responsive and satisfying. The landscapes are beautiful. And the fundamental gameplay loops remain beyond reproach. Ocarina of Time serves as the foundational blueprint for 3D dungeon puzzles in Zelda. Nearly 30 years later, they still feel remarkably clever, but my fondness for them is closer to the kind of nostalgic recognition I might feel while looking back through the handwritten notes in an old yearbook. You kinda had to be thereÂ back in 1998 to get the full effect.

Being there in 2026 with the remake, I’m surprised just how much of the original has been kept intact. While fans pore over all of the minute differences and pick apart the changes, I’m just a little bit disappointed by how much doesn’t feel new. The combat is mostly the same. The enemies function very similarly. And the side content appears to be more or less the same from the original.

If I didn’t already know the contours of everything you can do in the game, I’m sure it would be thrilling to be discovering all of the arcane secrets and connections for the first time (my kids would rather play friendslop). But with no Master Quest mode at launch, or additional bonus dungeons that iterate on modern design sensibilities and all of the lessons Nintendo has taught players in the intervening 28 years, the overall experience has been a bit hollow for me.

Nintendo may be planning to add that type of thing in future DLC. I’m not sure there’s any benefit to waiting, especially when the magic of sweeping millennial nostalgia is in full force at launch. For now I’m delighted but conflicted. I’d recommend the Ocarina of Time remake as the best way to play the game without reservation. I just wish more of it felt like the first time playing Ocarina of Time. But that’s my problem, not the game’s.

There is a lot for Tom Holland to consider when doing his own stunts in a Spider-Man film. For instance, there are the massive heights, the serious gymnastics skills needed and the potential of a broken bone that would delay a tight shooting schedule for an entire crew. Yet it seems like Holland and his co-stars had a unique fear when he was wearing the Spidey suit, and it had to do with the very real possibility of him getting sick in it, and the danger it may pose if he did.

During an interview on Josh Horowitz's Happy Sad Confused podcast, the host showed Holland an interview clip from the host in which Zendaya expressed her nervousness over him vomiting in his movie costume. Considering the amount of upside-down stunt work required from the Marvel star, potentially getting sick wasn’t out of the question. And if he did get sick, would he suffocate due to how constricting that suit was? When Holland was shown that video of his now-wife as well as co-star Jacob Batalon talking about it, he agreed with her:

It makes sense that both of the movie stars thought about this, especially considering that if this did happen, Holland couldn’t simply pull the mask off. The suit was one piece for the most part, so the head wouldn’t just easily come off. It was very constricting and may pose a real danger if the actor did throw up during a stunt sequence. Even with hundreds of crew members watching Holland with a careful eye, such a concern doesn’t feel completely unfounded.

While Holland admitted to thinking about this, he also revealed that about a potential solution. However, this particular method wouldn't have been so smooth. The Odyssey star explained: If such a thing happened, engineering with the newer suits made things a lot safer. Also considering he’d ripped the Spidey suit easily before, he knew he’d be okay. He explained:

It was definitely something that crossed my mind. I think that in reality I knew that if that did happen, I could pull the eyes out, grab the eye tray and I could just rip the — there's a rip cord. There's an emergency. It's not designed that way, but I'm pretty sure I could have done that. But, now, in the new suit, having worked with Tobey and Andrew and seeing the amount of engineering that went into their comfortability, I have a zip at the back of my head, which allows me to take the mask off to breathe.

As cool as the Spider-Man suits have looked on camera over the years, not all of them have always been constructed in ways that are convenient for the actor inside. Tom Holland has even easily ripped his Spidey-suit before. However, by the time he was working on Brand New Day, the possibility of Holland throwing up in his outfit wasn't as much of a concern:

But, now, in the new suit, having worked with Tobey [Maguire] and Andrew [Garfield] and seeing the amount of engineering that went into their comfortability, I have a zip at the back of my head, which allows me to take the mask off to breathe.

Thankfully, despite that key update, such a situation didn't happen, and the Spidey suit remained intact and vomit-free while stunt sequences were done. This is actually pretty impressive, considering how often Holland has done his own stunts while playing Spider-Man for 10 years.

While his co-stars expressed fear that he was getting too old to be doing his own stunts, the actor continued to participate in stunts for Brand New Day, and if Tom Cruise has anything to say about it, an actor truly never too old to do your own stunts. Holland is only 30, and I still think he could still pull off some sick (no pun intended) stunts in another Spidey flick.

You can see Tom Holland doing most of his own stunts clean and sickness-free in Spider-Man: Brand New Day, which is currently available to purchase on digital platforms. It’s one of the buzziest films on the 2026 movie schedule, so make sure to check it out. Fans of the franchise can also check out previous Spidey films now with a Disney+ subscription.

DJI may be best known for its drones and camera equipment, but the company has also been expanding into portable power, with the Power 2000 being its most capable standalone power station yet. Essentially a large rechargeable battery, it's designed to provide electricity wherever you might need it, whether that's on a camping trip, at a job site, during an outdoor movie night, or at home when the power goes out. And if you've been considering one for any of those situations, the Power 2000 is currently down to $749.99 from its original $1,299 price, taking nearly $550 off what would otherwise be a fairly expensive investment.

It's about the size of a carry-on suitcase and weighs close to 50 pounds, so it's not something you'd strap to your back, but it fits easily in a car trunk. The battery itself is built to last, rated for 4,000 charges before it starts losing any noticeable capacity. Performance-wise, DJI says the 2,048Wh capacity can keep a refrigerator running for up to 40 hours during a home power outage, charge a laptop 18 times, or power a projector for 18 hours. Those numbers line up with what you’d expect from a unit this size, and they make it useful for both emergencies and planned outdoor use.

You also get a solid mix of ports—there are three AC outlets, a 30-amp port for heavier appliances or RV setups, multiple USB-C ports (including a 140W option for laptops), and DJI’s own SDC ports for direct drone charging. If you use DJI gear, that alone makes life easier in the field, notes this Mashable review. Recharging is also fast for a battery this size. Plugged into a wall outlet, it can go from empty to full in about 90 minutes. You can also top it up with solar panels or from your car, which makes it workable for longer trips. Rounding out its features is its companion app, which lets you check its battery level from your phone without having to walk over to it, a small thing that turns out to be pretty convenient. Note that this unit has no built-in light, which is something many competing power stations include.

#3707. Kaia Gerber Shares Candid Quote About Grief After Presley Gerber's Death

Kaia Gerber is reflecting on the grieving process after brother Presley Gerber’s death.

Kaia, 25, shared a photo of a stack of books to her Instagram on Sunday, November 8, alongside a quote from Joan Didion’s The Year of Magical Thinking.

“Grief, when it comes, is nothing we expect it to be. Grief has no distance. Grief comes in waves, paroxysms, sudden apprehensions that weaken the knees and blind the eyes and obliterate the dailiness of life,” the quote read.

The post was uploaded by Kaia and the Library Science official Instagram account, a joint book program established by the actress and Alyssa Reeder. The upload comes less than two months after news broke that Presley died at age 27.

In September, the Santa Monica Police Department told Us officers responded to a call regarding a possible overdose at the sober living facility Resolutions Living. Authorities found an unresponsive adult male at the scene. (Presley had previously been candid about his mental health and addiction struggles.)

“The Los Angeles County Department of Medical Examiner has identified the individual as Presley Gerber, 27,” authorities said in a statement. “SMPD detectives are investigating the death as a suspected overdose. At this time, there is no indication of foul play. The official cause and manner of death will be determined by the Los Angeles County Department of Medical Examiner.”

One day later, the Los Angeles County Medical Examiner confirmed that Presley’s body was “ready for release.” Presley’s cause of death was “deferred,” per records viewed by Us, and his body was later cremated.

His death has since resulted in an investigation into the sober living facility after a reform advocate with no relation to Presley reportedly filed a formal complaint. Page Six later reported in October that the California Department of Health Care Services (DHCS) determined there wasn’t enough evidence to substantiate any wrongdoing on the part of the Resolutions Living treatment facility.

Presley, the son of Cindy Crawford and Rande Gerber, was honored in a statement by his family in October.

“We are beyond heartbroken to lose our beloved son and brother. We feel so blessed to have had Presley in our lives for 27 years,” the family wrote at the time. “He is a sweet, beautiful soul who loved and is loved, now and forever.”

In general, the dialogue hints that this mystery mask makes them uneasy, with someone even calling it “otherworldly.” Austin John theorizes that this is dialogue coded in for a future amiibo figure featuring a character from Majoraâs Mask, possibly Skull Kid, and that this amiibo could be coming out alongside a Switch 2 Majoraâs Mask remake.Â

#3704. Laura Loomer, Elon Musk, George Santos, and More React to Election Night: “I Hope Everyone Is Learning Arabic”

The midterm elections marked a night of historic firsts: Adam Hamilton became the first Democratic senator elected in Kansas in nearly 100 years; Chris Pappas is now the first openly gay man to be voted into the Senate; Keisha Lance Bottoms is the first Black woman to be elected as a US governor; Bentley Hudgins is the first transgender and nonbinary lawmaker to be voted into the Georgia General Assembly—the list goes on.

How better to chronicle a generational evening in US history than on social media? Our founding fathers recounted watershed moments via post riders and printed broadsides; in the mid-19th century, dispatches were sent via the Pony Express. President Lincoln’s shooting was rushed to the public via Morse code tapped over the wires, and during World War I, we utilized undersea telegraph cables. Yet in our long history spanning radio broadcasts, satellite television, and smoke signals, nothing has quite captured the zeitgeist like an X post.

“CNN is now saying the national anthem has been changed to a reggaeton cover of Pink Pony Club,” tweeted one user last night, right as the media joined a chorus of policy analysts and pundits to announce a new dawn as Democrats took control of Congress—a blue wave. Or rather, a blue tsunami.

Social media users across the country then took to X to mourn, deny, or celebrate the victory. Yet amid the cacophony of social media’s tweets, posts, replies, comments, and reels, the most notorious influencer grew shockingly quiet: President Donald Trump himself. Despite posting a half-hearted image of a MAGA-red hat reading “VETO,” Trump has not said much online in the hours following the victory.

In the months leading up to the midterms, social media did more than simply sway victories. In fact, it propelled candidates like Jon Ossoff to the forefront through short-form vertical videos, made contenders such as Abdul El-Sayed go viral through clips set to songs like Eminem’s 2010 hit “Not Afraid,” and directed Gen Z focus to key races through memes (“TEXAS JUST WENT BLUE. PUT PRONOUNS BACK IN YOUR BIO NOW,” New York City Council member Chi Ossé posted in his Instagram Stories last night).

More than three quarters of young adults relied on social media or platforms like YouTube as a source for their midterm election news this year. An astounding 67% of millennials also got the lowdown from content creators. Call it absurd, call it brain rot, or call it sensational: There’s no doubt that social media has become a phenomenon, and the Twitterverse is still alive and well in 2026.

#3703. Nick Jonas Admits He 'Resents' His Diabetes Diagnosis in Candid Open Letter

Nick Jonas is reflecting on navigating diabetes more than two decades after receiving his diagnosis.

“It’s funny how often we talk,” Jonas, 34, wrote in an open letter as part of Dexcom’s A Letter to Diabetes initiative. “Staring at my phone to see where my glucose is. Reaching for my pump to bolus because I’m about to eat something with 17 carbs. Those are just a couple of the hundreds of little decisions I make every week.”

He continued, “Most people never notice them. But they add up to a real relationship, because that’s what diabetes is. It’s an ongoing conversation between your body, your mind and your devices.”

The Jonas Brothers star, who is now a father, shared that the “unpredictability” of diabetes “threw” him when he initially received his diagnosis in 2005 at the age of 13. (Jonas and wife Priyanka Chopra Jonas welcomed their daughter, Malti, via surrogate in 2022.)

“I’d built my whole life around this unrealistic structure and belief that I was in control. You took that apart over the years, bit by bit,” he wrote. “Part of me is grateful I learned that lesson. Part of me resents you for it. Full stop. There are days I wonder what life would feel like without you.”

Despite resenting the disease for its impact on his life, Jonas also reflected on the positives of learning to live with Type 1 diabetes.

“I always struggled to feel like I belonged anywhere. At school, I felt misunderstood. In most circles, for that matter. Through my childhood and youth, that was the theme. It wasn’t until I started talking openly about life with type 1, and meeting other people who were living it too, that I finally felt like I belonged somewhere,” he explained, adding that he never wanted to be seen as a “victim.”

From Jonas’ perspective, his candidness about this journey may help others see someone like him “out there living their dreams.”

“I share my story for the 13-year-old who just got diagnosed and is lying in a hospital bed, scared to death. I want them to be able to look up and see someone out there living their dreams while managing all of this, every single day,” he said. “So thank you, old friend, for the lessons I never asked for. I’m going to keep sharing my story and telling the truth, so someone out there feels a little less alone.”

Supper Mario Broth, the internet’s number one guy for obscure Mario facts, has shared that he’s in failing health but will continue to bring fans Mario morsels to sup upon until the last flag falls. In a post on social media, Brothâwho has not shared his real name and says he prefers to go by Brothâsaid that despite living a healthy lifestyle, he has heart failure and that his prognosis gives him a 2/3 chance to survive a year.

I am scared I will soon not be able to see Mario again. However, I promise that until that day arrives, I will always be here, posting Mario facts. Thank you all so much for your support through the years.

— Supper Mario Broth (@mariobrothblog.bsky.social) 2026-11-08T20:21:37.669Z

Broth also says that one of the symptoms of his heart failure diagnosis is retinopathy, or the slow degradation of his eyesight. “Since being able to see well is fundamental to my ability to both myself research Mario games and compile the discoveries of others, this may affect my ability to run Supper Mario Broth in the future,” Broth said. “But only blindness or death will result in me no longer posting Mario facts.”

In 2024, Broth posted that his blog was in danger of shutting down due to strained finances in the wake of his mother’s passing. After an impassioned plea for help, the internet rallied around Broth, providing him with enough support that he said he’d be able to continue the Supper Mario Broth project indefinitely.

If you’ve ever wanted weird, obscure, fun, or possibly haunting facts about Mario, Supper Mario Broth was your guy. The Nintendo blogger has been around since at least 2012 posting Mario ephemera gleaned from the plumber’s many games, comics, TV shows, movies, advertising materials, and more. Broth is the one who brought us the Yoshi’s Island glitch that will stop the game for 25 minutes. He told us that in Super Mario Odyssey, Bowser gets scared when Mario has his nipples out. He’s also the guy who fucked us all up with the forbidden (though not canon) knowledge that 1-UP mushrooms grow from dead Marios.

He is possibly the only person in the world who loves and knows Mario as much as Shigeru Miyamoto, and potentially losing him is not only a blow to Mario scholarship but the cool gaming internet as a whole.Â

Broth said that despite his prognosis, he will continue to maintain the blog for as long as he can. “I hope with all my (failing) heart that I can continue doing this for years to come,” he said. “And if I should one day stop posting: thank you very much for reading.”

Derek Hough And A DWTS Winner Have The Same Prediction About One Star Making The Finale (And I Totally Agree)

Fans Aren’t Sure If A Survivor 51 Castaway Is Getting A Winner’s Edit Or Being Set Up For Heartbreak

Survivor's Brady Got Asked About The Peeing Thing (But I Can't Get Over How Many Times He Said Brody)

Unlock instant access to exclusive member features.

I feel better about Mike than at least three other players.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Earlier this week, I was talking to a few of my friends about Survivor 51, and I mentioned I thought Mike Pinsky could still win the game. They were absolutely shocked, and I can understand why. We’ve gotten confessional after confessional from the other players about how he’s a “bottom feeder” and a “sponge” and uses “bullying tactics.” It obviously hasn’t been a dream first half of the game for the Yankees employee, but as someone who follows how the show is edited very closely, I see some reasons for optimism. In fact, I think there are four players we can completely write off, and he is not one of them.

Before I get into the three players I’m done with, let’s talk about Mike for a few paragraphs and why I still believe there’s a chance for him. Let’s start with confessionals. He only has eighteen confessionals for the season, which puts him behind seven players still left in the game, but when you actually dive into the specifics, it’s not that bad.

He’s only gone to Tribal Council three total times, which means he hasn’t been a necessary part of the A-plot during most episodes. Despite that, he’s still gotten at least one confessional during every single episode, and during the last two episodes, he’s gotten ten confessionals, which is behind only Eric, Jelly and Sharonda. The show has found ways to include him, even when it hasn’t been necessary.

The content itself also hasn’t been as consistently negative as you’d think. We all remember the confessionals from Thien An, Kristin, Kilby, Brady and others burying him and calling him a “floater” and every other name in the book. Obviously those are bad, but we’ve also gotten confessionals from other people saying they want to work with him. Jelly said she’s been playing the game with Mike since day one and wants to rekindle that relationship. Eric said he’s building a real bond with Mike both inside and outside the game.

In addition, we have gotten some really good confessionals from Mike himself, ones that almost sound like winner confessionals. Two episodes ago, he told us he feels like if he can just get to the merge, he could win the game. This past episode, the show aired his voting confessional where he said the future of his game is related to that vote going his way. Well, that vote did go his way, and he did make the merge and start finding new allies.

To be clear, I’m not saying you should gamble all the money in your bank account on Mike. He’s still a huge underdog. The show has dunked on him more in the edit than any winner since the infamous All-I-Gabler. There are plenty of reasons to be very skeptical about him winning, starting with how many players have said they don’t like him, but there are just too many hints of positivity for me to sell completely. He just won immunity and wrangled all the votes needed to get Brady out. He’s got a strong relationship with Jelly, who seems like she’s poised to go deep in the game. He’s had some dynamite confessionals talking about his path to winning and his game strategy. There are signs of life.

Unfortunately, I can’t see those same signs of life for three other players, and unlike Mike, I am ready to write them off at this point. I can’t see any scenario in which Cristian Chavez wins the game. Objectively, it seems like he’s playing a really strong game out there. He’s got a bunch of close relationships, and some eliminated castaways during their exit press have mentioned that he’s a really shrewd strategist. He’s been in no real danger in any episode, but the edit is just not there to support a win. Every single winner since Survivor 41 has had at least one confessional during every episode. He’s had multiple episodes with zero confessionals and is tied for the lowest on the entire season with just ten. If he was the winner, wouldn’t the show, you know, give us his perspective a little more?

The same can also be said for Thien An Nguyen and Carter Krull. Thien An is tied with Cristian among all the remaining players for last in confessionals with ten total, and she also had an episode where she got skunked. In addition, it feels like half of her confessionals have been about how much she personally dislikes Mike. During 50, most of Charlie’s entire edit was depicted almost exclusively through the lens of him hating Rizo. Thien An is getting the same treatment. It’s like she just pops in long enough to fire up some middle fingers at Mike and disappears into the background again. It’s funny but it’s also annoying because we know she was responsible for the Pantsless Patt blindside and seems to be one of the better strategic players on the board. I'd love to hear from her more.

I’ve also lost all faith in Carter as a potential winner too. He’s gotten a lot more content than Cristian and Thien An, but most of his content has been camp life shenanigans. We got some great scenes of him building a sack swing with Brady and Mike. We got some great scenes of him getting confused while trying to find an advantage and then maybe accidentally on purpose mutinying. He’s gotten his character moments and has turned into a fan favorite, but we just haven’t heard from him very much strategically. He had one standout episode with ten confessionals, but outside of that, he’s only had eight confessionals if you don’t count that one episode, and he’s also been blanked twice. He’s not winning.

I feel very confident in eliminating all three of those players. The show’s edit just doesn’t make any sense if they win. They’ve been background characters far too often, and there have been too many key moments in which we haven’t gotten their perspective. It’s not just that I would be shocked if they won, it’s that I would feel like the show was edited poorly if they won.

To me, Mike is quite clearly ahead of that group by a large margin. Instead, I’d put him on a different tier with a few other players who have been more consistent parts of the show but also have clear warning signs to their edits. I’m thinking of someone like Eric who has gotten a ton of confessionals but also is frequently shown annoying the other castaways. I’m thinking of someone like Maggie who is a consistent presence but hasn’t been given as much credit in the edit for some big moves, most prominently sniping out Linnea. Like Mike, they’re definitely still alive, but there are valid reasons to be skeptical.

The goal for the Survivor editors is never to tell the most accurate possible story. Instead, it’s always to tell the most engaging possible story that also accurately tells what happened. That’s an important distinction, and it’s the reason why I’m willing to write off Cristian, Thien An and Carter, but I’m still willing to hold out some hope for Mike.

#3700. This Autonomous Camera Robot Is My New Best Friend

Like any pure-hearted geek, I've wanted to own a droid ever since I saw Star Wars as a kid. Now, I actually have one: It's Beni, a new gadget from Mondo Robotics, and it has me saying, "Artoo who?" It's not just my Upgrade of the Week; it's possibly the upgrade of my life.

Beni is an all-terrain camera robot that was born as a project on Kickstarter, but unlike so many other Kickstarted projects, it's actually really cool. It takes 4K video while autonomously following its subject wherever they go. If you want to get action footage, there's no need to hassle with a tripod or another person: You can control it with a remote, or you can make it follow you. It can also be set to track you from the side or circle you, and you can adjust what it is doing from the app or remote control on the fly, so with minimal effort, there's no limit to the kind of elaborate shots it can pull off. Plus it's adorable. Just look at this little guy:

Being cute wouldn't matter if Beni was just a gimmick, but the footage it takes is actually really impressive. Check out this clip, which I recorded with no planning of any sort; I just locked Beni's camera on this skater and told it to follow him wherever:

See how smoothly it glides over the uneven concrete? How effortlessly it handles inclines? I even launched it off a huge ramp and it landed on the other side, righted itself, and got back to business.

Here's an example of the kind of footageyou'll get when you put it in "circle you" mode (and again, this was recorded with no prior planning):

The way it just slides under that bench? Come ON. That's just slick.

Yes, Beni is a slightly silly product, but as slightly silly products go, it's pretty inarguably awesome. Here is a short list of things I love about Beni:

It's super easy-to-use. I got it up and running moments after taking it out of the box and downloading the app. You can easily figure out how it works on the fly.

It's a multi-terrain robot. You can get an extra set of bigger, beefier wheels, but even with the stock tires, this thing worked great on uneven concrete, grass, and dirt.

It's rugged. While Beni does have obstacle detection ability, it runs into things a lot anyway, but that's not a problem. Beni can take massive, epic spills, slam into walls, and get kicked by children, and it will right itself and proceed on without a hitch. It's amazing to watch.

It actually works the way you expect it to. I know that's a low bar to clear, but it's rare for a flashy piece of tech to actually do what it says it promises, and Beni does.

It's adorable. A lot of work went into making Beni as friendly-looking as possible—it does tricks, blinks its "eyes," responds to gestures, and you can even give him a little baseball cap. Beni's vibe is positive.

It's great for social interaction. If you have a little robot following you around, people will want to talk to you. I'm not a huge fan of people, but if you want to make friends at the park, this robot will at least open the door.

It's not as expensive as you might imagine. Beni will run you $750 for the base model, and $899 for the "Explore Combo" with larger wheels, a charging stand, and a little hat. While $750 isn't cheap, for what you get, it's actually a pretty solid deal. Everything costs a fortune now anyway! You deserve a robot.

Beni isn't quite ready to make its debut yet. Right now, you can pre-order one on Mondo Robotics site, with a release planned for some time in early November. This is the company's first product, so it's not yet clear if Beni will ever be sold via third-party retailers like Amazon.

#3699. Mike Tirico Announces He'll Miss SNF Game Due to an Unspecified Health Issue

NBC’s Mike Tirico will be absent from Sunday Night Football while navigating a “health issue.”

“Unfortunately, I will have to miss tonight’s game in Chicago due to a health issue,” Tirico, 59, wrote in a statement shared via NBC’s social media on Sunday, November 8. “I look forward to watching tonight and can’t wait to be back with Cris, Melissa and the rest of our SNF team next Sunday night in Cincinnati.”

He continued, “Noah Eagle will call tonight’s game with Cris Collinsworth and Melissa Stark.”

No further details were shared about Tirico’s health. The lead NBC play-by-play announcer was scheduled to broadcast the Chicago Bears and Tampa Bay Buccaneers game on Sunday.

The matchup was set to be his 300th NFL broadcast. Tirico has been the lead Sunday Night Football play-by-play announcer since 2022, when he replaced legendary announcer Al Michaels. He is also known for his commentary during NBA games and the Olympics.

In 2025, Tirico made headlines when he pulled out of covering the 151st Kentucky Derby after suffering a “significant” allergic reaction. Host and sports reporter Ahmed Fareed took on the role in Tirico’s absence.

“Hate being a scratch after making the starting gate @KentuckyDerby. Just a significant reaction to my nut allergy. If you have one you know how it can knock you down,” Tirico wrote via X at the time. “Profound thanks to @ChurchillDowns for their care. And to our amazing @nbcsports horse racing family. Especially Randy, Jerry & Ahmed Fareed So lucky to have @SyracuseU fam step in and do such a great job🍊.”

Days after the Kentucky Derby, Tirico shared an update on his health and assured fans he was feeling “fine” after the scare.

“I’ve had a nut allergy my whole life and I’m usually very, very careful. … I ate something that had a nut in it and had a nut allergy, causing your throat and your nose all that stuff to kind of clog up and swell. It affects your breathing a little bit, so [I] wasn’t feeling well, couldn’t go on with the show, took an EpiPen shot, got treated by EMTs, felt better about 8, 9 o’clock came along, but it takes a long while to get out of your system,” Tirico said during an appearance on Today in 2025. “And thank goodness Ahmed Fareed, who’s great, was there and filled in more than abley. The show went on without us.”
