#3589. 25 Best Directors Of All Time, Ranked

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

Ranking the best directors of all time is a formidable task. How do you weigh a director's output against their influence? Ultimately, the question is who has left the most lasting impression on film culture, and why.

Making a list like this also means confronting the industry's realities. You'll notice a dismal underrepresentation of directors of color, women, and queer filmmakers compared to the overwhelming majority of entries: white men.

Hollywood, and the filmmaking industry writ large, have historically diminished the voices of marginalized filmmakers, limiting their opportunities to create, distribute, and receive recognition for their work. When those opportunities have disproportionately gone to the same insular group, it's no surprise their work has come to dominate the cinematic canon. Hopefully, future renditions of this list will reflect a greater appreciation of historically overlooked filmmakers and the continued emergence of exciting, diverse voices pushing the medium forward.

For now, the directors on this list reflect film history's achievements and the inequities that have shaped it. Here are the 25 best directors of all time, ranked.

John Carpenter may not watch his own movies, but for the rest of us, he's left an indelible mark on genre cinema. He made "Halloween" in 1978 for a reported $325,000, scoring one of horror's most recognizable piano themes in three days and drafting a slasher blueprint: the ominous quiet of suburbia shattered by violence, all in gorgeous Scope framing. That's just one of his essential films, as "Assault on Precinct 13," "Escape From New York," and "The Thing" have helped cement his legacy.

Hollywood never quite knew what to do with Carpenter, not that he cared. "Big Trouble in Little China" flopped before becoming a respected cult object. "They Live" screamed its anti-consumerist messaging to the rafters inside a winking sci-fi B-movie, featuring one of the longest and goofiest fight scenes ever filmed. Few filmmakers have maintained such an unmistakable sensibility as Carpenter's stylish, innovative takes on horror and pulp.

Billy Wilder fled terror in Europe and arrived in Hollywood with limited English, eventually becoming one of the town's sharpest writers. As a director, he constantly hopped genres without a hitch. "Double Indemnity," co-written with Raymond Chandler, helped define film noir; "The Lost Weekend" won Best Picture and Best Director at the Academy Awards for its unflinching look at alcoholism; the Gothic Hollywood nightmare of "Sunset Boulevard" scandalized the industry and aged into one of the most essential showbiz movies ever.

"Some Like It Hot," starring Marilyn Monroe, was named the greatest American comedy by the AFI. "The Apartment" threaded office-politics farce through a funny, emotional, deeply bittersweet story of loneliness, heartbreak, and workplace exploitation, going on to take home Best Picture. Wilder's films were often cynical, funny, and deeply humane all at once. If you need a place to start, we ranked 14 of his best movies.

Christopher Nolan's legacy is already set in stone as a modern-day showman, and he's perhaps the last director who can conjure blockbuster events based on his name alone. His modest breakout "Memento" hinted at his cerebral ambitions. "The Dark Knight" elevated the gritty, tactile superhero movie into a new blockbuster standard, and "Inception" cemented his reputation as a purveyor of brainy yet crowd-pleasing big-budget spectacle. Of course, he is also the movie theater's loudest and most ardent evangelist, championing IMAX cameras, real film stock, and practical stunts.

His overwhelming ambition has never insulated him from criticism though, as detractors harp on cold characters, muddy sound mixes, and an unholy amount of exposition. But to see "Interstellar," "Dunkirk," or "The Odyssey" in a true IMAX presentation is to immerse yourself in the palpable vision of a man who knows exactly how to stage a set-piece. To watch "Oppenheimer" is to be amazed at how he can turn a three-hour biopic of men talking in rooms into something as high-octane as his thrillers. Nolan is in a league all his own, so we had a hard time ranking his movies.

Nobody captures the sensorial experience of longing quite like Wong Kar-wai. The Hong Kong auteur, often working with cinematographer Christopher Doyle, built a visual language of romantic yearning from neon smears, slow-motion blurs, and step-printing warps of time and motion. Countless filmmakers have chased the ineffable quality he summons in his films about the aches and desires of the human experience, especially his standout film "Chungking Express," anchored by Tony Leung's exquisite features. The film helped make him an international name, with a boost from Quentin Tarantino, whose short-lived Rolling Thunder Pictures label brought it to American theaters, and "Happy Together" earned him Best Director at Cannes in 1997.

But it's "In the Mood for Love" that gave him legendary status. Pairing Tony Leung with Maggie Cheung as neighbors in 1962 Hong Kong who discover their spouses are having an affair, he turns it into a romance of pure, repressed feeling. It's the epitome of the entire Wong Kar-wai project, and it's the movie that has cemented his legacy. It also landed at #5 in Sight & Sound's 2022 critics' poll.

Robert Altman wasn't one to conform to Hollywood's tidy, controlled storytelling. A former bomber pilot who cut his teeth on industrial films and television, he broke through with "M*A*S*H," a profane, anti-authoritarian war comedy that won the top prize at Cannes in 1970. He developed a signature style built on overlapping dialogue, wandering zoom lenses, and enormous ensemble casts, often capturing multiple conversations simultaneously and extracting moments of clarity from the chaos. He adapted this style across the gamut of genres: "McCabe & Mrs. Miller" envisioned the Western as a hazy character study; "The Long Goodbye" subverted the noir by turning it into a shaggy, meandering ramble; and "Nashville" makes a compelling case for being the great American movie of the 1970s.

After the troubled "Popeye" in 1980, he spent years on the margins, working in theater and low-budget stage adaptations, before roaring back with "The Player," his biting Hollywood satire, followed by "Short Cuts" and "Gosford Park." He was nominated for Best Director five times, never won, but finally received an honorary Oscar in 2006, months before his death at 81. Altman may not have spent much time analyzing his own films, but a wealth of genius remains.

Before becoming an architect of cinematic epics, David Lean worked his way up from studio cutting rooms to become one of British film's finest editors. The training shows in the precision of everything he would go on to shoot. After co-directing "In Which We Serve" with Noël Coward, he made "Brief Encounter," a beautifully felt railway-station romance of aching restraint, whose DNA is evident in beloved movies such as "Before Sunset" and "The Bridges of Madison County."

It was later that he would prove his gift for scale. "The Bridge on the River Kwai" won Best Picture and Best Director, but, of course, it's "Lawrence of Arabia" that turned his name into shorthand for grandeur — a movie with a rare perfect Metacritic score. That film alone earns him a spot here, even without his other wonderfully helmed features, which all reveal a filmmaker attuned to the most crucial tenets of storytelling.

Not just one of the most influential comedy stars in history, and one of the most famous entertainers to ever work in Hollywood, many of Charles "Charlie" Chaplin's greatest successes were helmed by the man himself. From London poverty and the music-hall stage, he began experimenting with directing at Keystone in 1914 with "Twenty Minutes of Love." "Caught in the Rain" followed, his first film with sole directing responsibility. From there, he spent his career proving how his formal prowess complemented his physical dexterity.

His silent and early sound masterpieces include "The Kid," "The Gold Rush," "City Lights," "Modern Times," and "The Great Dictator," his first full talkie, in which he lampooned Hitler while the United States was still neutral. Such boldness had consequences: While sailing for London in 1952, amid the Red Scare, the government revoked his re-entry permit, and he settled in Switzerland, later returning for an honorary Oscar in 1972.

Howard Hawks left enduring imprints across seemingly limitless genres. He helped define the violent gangster picture with "Scarface." He directed two of the best screwball comedies of all time, "Bringing Up Baby" and "His Girl Friday." He made the tough-minded adventure "Only Angels Have Wings." He paired Humphrey Bogart with Lauren Bacall twice, in "To Have and Have Not" and "The Big Sleep," creating one of the most seductive cinematic pairings ever seen on screen. "Red River" and "Rio Bravo" can both claim a place among Hollywood's most essential Westerns.

Hawks did it all. He accentuates the material with an invisible style: eye-level camerawork, unfussy staging, and a preoccupation with professionals who earn each other's respect, including strong-willed women who demand to be treated as equals. He was the kind of Hollywood workman who made masterpieces by simply showing up and understanding the job.

Federico Fellini began as a cartoonist and gag writer, then he co-wrote for Roberto Rossellini on "Rome, Open City" and "Paisan," foundational works of Italian neorealism, before broadening his scope. "La Strada" and "Nights of Cabiria," fables of the poor and discarded, announced his talent, but it was "La Dolce Vita" that cemented his international reputation and became one of the greatest Italian films ever made — it was also Roger Ebert's favorite movie of all time. The Palme d'Or winner follows Marcello Mastroianni through Rome's decadent nightlife, capturing the estranged emotional perspective of a hollow, meaningless pursuit of glamour.

From there, he turned inward. "8½" is perhaps his most famous film, the definitive movie about a director paralyzed by his own creative crisis, blending memory, fantasy, and self-doubt in a way self-reflective directors have tried to imitate in Fellini's wake. Later came the carnivalesque "Fellini Satyricon," "Roma," and the nostalgic "Amarcord," another Oscar winner. His singular vision earned him a word of his own: "Felliniesque."

In a decade, Francis Ford Coppola made a run of films that may be the greatest in history. He fought a studio that didn't want Marlon Brando or Al Pacino in what would be his seminal, culture-shattering "The Godfather." He followed that up with two masterpieces in 1974: "The Conversation," which took home the top prize at Cannes, and "The Godfather Part II," the rare sequel that exceeded its predecessor and became the first sequel to win Best Picture. "Apocalypse Now" followed, after a legendarily disastrous shoot in the Philippines so troubled it inspired its own documentary, "Hearts of Darkness."

That run alone earns Coppola his place among the greats, even if all that risk-taking nearly broke him. The expensive flop "One from the Heart" crippled his Zoetrope studio, and he spent years making movies to pay off debts. Even so, he kept swinging, from "Rumble Fish" to the operatic "Bram Stoker's Dracula," and bankrolled the truly zany "Megalopolis" himself, reportedly with money from his wine business. Whatever you make of it, few directors have been this ambitious for this long.

Spike Lee, for all his prolificacy, can be an uneven director — there's a reason we were able to list his eight best and seven worst movies — but he's responsible for some of the most important American movies ever made, particularly in his exploration of Black American life. Arriving with "She's Gotta Have It," he would soon follow with his critically acclaimed drama "Do the Right Thing," a loving yet raging cultural firestorm of fractured societal relationships that refuses to placate its audience.

His refusal to back down from his beliefs comes through in a brash, flashy style that is instantly recognizable, particularly in his signature "double dolly" shot. But he can be flexible too. "Malcolm X" showed his epic reach, "Inside Man" his mainstream chops, and "BlacKkKlansman" his insight into how yesterday's politics collide with today's. Consistency be damned, he's an essential component of American filmmaking.

Agnès Varda came to cinema as a still photographer with almost no film training, and she made her debut, "La Pointe Courte," in 1955, years before the French New Wave she's often credited with anticipating. She was one of the few women in a scene dominated by cinephile men, and she stood out by making her sensibility entirely her own: curious, playful, and warmly attentive to ordinary people. "Cléo from 5 to 7" is a luminous examination of a pop singer drifting through Paris as she awaits medical test results, while "Vagabond," which won the Golden Lion at Venice, is an unsentimental portrait of a young drifter found dead in a ditch.

Varda also slipped freely between fiction and documentary, often blending the two. "The Gleaners and I" found poetry in scavengers and discarded produce, while "Faces Places," co-directed with the artist JR, earned her a Best Documentary Feature nomination at the 90th Academy Awards in 2018, making the 89-year-old Varda the oldest Oscar nominee in Academy history at the time. She kept working until her death in 2019 and made waves with critics throughout her career, including being among the highest-rated female-directed movies on Metacritic.

Hayao Miyazaki is animation's most devoted craftsman, introducing generations of children internationally to the detailed artistry of Japanese animation while also exposing them to challenging, scary, and profound ideas that have helped prepare them for adulthood. He co-founded Studio Ghibli (whose films we've ranked) in 1985 with Isao Takahata and Toshio Suzuki, and made a run of films that treated childhood as serious business: the gentle fable "My Neighbor Totoro," the coming-of-age story of a young witch discovering her purpose in "Kiki's Delivery Service," and the ecological fantasy epic "Princess Mononoke."

Then came "Spirited Away," which won the Golden Bear in Berlin and the Oscar for Best Animated Feature, and it was Japan's highest-grossing film for nearly two decades. The free-wheeling, wafting nature of Miyazaki's films comes from his unconventional process: He storyboards without a finished script, discovering the heart of the films as he draws. After returning from retirement to make "The Boy and the Heron," which earned him another Oscar for Best Animated Feature, Miyazaki remains creatively active well into his eighties. His extraordinary animation is a legacy any filmmaker could only dream of.

Andrei Tarkovsky made only seven features, each with seismic influence across generations. He once called filmmaking "sculpting in time," and that idea shapes his often abstruse yet spiritually profound work. As Ingmar Bergman once said, he invented a new language for film. Watching a Tarkovsky movie means being enraptured by its emotional depth, hidden within its mysteries.

His major works are must-sees. These include "Solaris," which turns Stanisław Lem's novel into a fractured meditation on memory and guilt; "Mirror," which weaves Tarkovsky's own childhood, newsreel footage, and his father Arseny's poetry into a chimerical collage; and "Stalker," one of the most influential and widely imitated sci-fi films ever made. Along with works such as "Andrei Rublev" and "Ivan's Childhood," Tarkovsky left behind a slim yet crucial filmography that helped define Soviet cinema and continues to influence filmmakers worldwide.

Sidney Lumet was a child actor on stage before becoming one of television's most active directors, and the discipline of working quickly and efficiently for television remained in his DNA. He put his TV work to good use with "12 Angry Men," his iconic pressure-cooker juror drama, which now stands as one of the best film debuts ever. He favored complex characters and sharp commentary on the modern world, as seen in movies like "Serpico," "Dog Day Afternoon," "Prince of the City," and "Network."

Lumet loved actors, rehearsing them like a stage company, and many of his stars delivered some of their best performances under his direction, from Al Pacino's sweaty bank robber in "Dog Day Afternoon" to Paul Newman's washed-up lawyer in "The Verdict." He made great movies until the end of his career, releasing "Before the Devil Knows You're Dead" at age 83, before his death in 2011.

Alfred Hitchcock earned the nickname "The Master of Suspense" for a reason. After honing his craft on British silent films and thrillers like "The 39 Steps" and "The Lady Vanishes," he crossed the Atlantic to work with producer David O. Selznick and made "Rebecca," which won Best Picture. However, since Best Picture statues go to a film's producers, Hitchcock would ultimately go 0-for-5 in the Best Director category.

Hitchcock's legacy has rested less on awards than on his ability to shock audiences. He made archetypal horror and thriller masterpieces, including "Rear Window," "North by Northwest," "Psycho," and "Vertigo," which would later topple "Citizen Kane" from the top of Sight & Sound's critics' poll in 2012, ending a 50-year reign. His genius endures to this day, and his films feel just as thrilling and transgressive as ever, which is fitting for the director with the most perfect movies, according to Metacritic.

It's often said that Joel and Ethan Coen are a directing duo who share a single brain, each completely in tune with the other's dry, morbid, gleefully caustic sense of humor and irony in their portrayals of people whose downfalls are their own making. They distilled the sensibility of their entire career in their debut neo-noir "Blood Simple" and kept that same mordant sensibility across genres and decades. From the screwball kidnapping farce "Raising Arizona" to the surrealistic Hollywood allegory "Barton Fink" to the breakout Minnesota nice-crime story "Fargo," which won a screenplay Oscar and Best Actress for Frances McDormand, nearly all of the Coens' films share a harmonious blend of dark comedy and drama.

Their mid-career run was just as strong: "No Country for Old Men" is one of the best neo-Westerns ever, while movies like "A Serious Man," "True Grit," and "Inside Llewyn Davis" continued to prove the success of their strange amalgamations of tenderness, humor, and bleak perceptions of reality. The Coens also pull career-best performances from their actors, so good that we had to rank the best of them. Their decision to pursue separate projects in recent years has only accentuated the miraculous consistency of their work together — and with the brothers now expressing plans to reunite behind the camera, there may yet be another chapter in one of cinema's great creative partnerships.

Any time you need a shock to the system, remember that Paul Thomas Anderson made "Boogie Nights" when he was just 26. Most recently in the spotlight for finally winning Best Picture, Best Director, and Best Adapted Screenplay for "One Battle After Another," his freewheeling riff on Thomas Pynchon's "Vineland," Anderson has spent years as your dedicated cinephile's de facto favorite contemporary director.

With a career defined by such formal bravado, how could he not be? Nearly all his films have defenders who call them masterpieces, from the three-hour interconnected melodrama epic "Magnolia" to "Punch-Drunk Love," which proved Adam Sandler's capability as a dramatic lead. Of course, it's "There Will Be Blood," one of Daniel Day-Lewis' best films, that tops many best-of-the-century lists, but his subsequent work, "The Master," "Phantom Thread," and "Licorice Pizza," is imbued with his radiant sensibility just as well. Anderson makes movies that buzz with pure cinematic brilliance.

Nothing captures David Lynch's sensibility better than the clip of him being asked to elaborate on why "Eraserhead" is his most spiritual movie, and him curtly replying, "No, I won't." For as routine as the term "Lynchian" has become when describing movies that are any shade of strange or surreal, the true ethos of Lynch's movies is that intangible quality that's hard to explain in the first place and nearly impossible to replicate. Even still, Lynch's filmography is diverse: the tender, Oscar-nominated "The Elephant Man," the misfired blockbuster "Dune," the unsettling revelations of suburban secrets in "Blue Velvet," and the surprising warmth of his G-rated, Disney-produced road movie "The Straight Story."

His legacy will be remembered mostly for "Mulholland Drive," a project initially conceived as a spinoff of his groundbreaking television series "Twin Peaks," which later evolved into a standalone ABC pilot that Lynch reworked into a film after the network passed on it, as well as his return to "Peaks" with "The Return" in 2017, perhaps the boldest television has ever been. Lynch sadly passed away in 2025, but he leaves behind a legacy of unsettling dreams and devoted compassion toward the human experience. No other voice will ever be like his.

Martin Scorsese is cinema's most passionate student and, increasingly, its most devoted steward and custodian, through work such as his World Cinema Project, which preserves, restores, and showcases neglected and underseen films from around the world. Raised in Little Italy, he was an asthmatic kid who spent his childhood in movie theaters and nearly became a priest before NYU film school pointed him elsewhere. Sin, guilt, and the hunger for redemption would color so many of his works: the raw street poetry of "Mean Streets," the Palme d'Or-winning "Taxi Driver," the bruising "Raging Bull," and "Goodfellas," one of the defining landmarks of gangster cinema.

At 83, he's still making some of his best work. Take a look at movies like "The Wolf of Wall Street," "Silence," "The Irishman," and "Killers of the Flower Moon" to see a director who has never lost his touch, continually finding new ways to explore his perspectives on faith, morality, and humanity through his unmistakable cinematic style. There is indeed an argument that Scorsese is our greatest living filmmaker.

Stanley Kubrick's legendary attention to detail casts an imposing shadow across film history. Though he may never have won a Best Director Oscar, the skill he exhibited across a diverse slate of masterpieces is, in effect, one of the greatest influences on his contemporaries and those who followed in his wake.

His films have become synonymous with filmmaking mastery, and yet it still manages to stun that the same man made the likes of "Dr. Strangelove," "2001: A Space Odyssey," "A Clockwork Orange," "Barry Lyndon," "The Shining," "Full Metal Jacket," and "Eyes Wide Shut." That's not even counting his impressive early work, which included "The Killing," "Paths of Glory," "Spartacus," and "Lolita." He may not be the most prolific director on this list, but the caliber of his work has earned him enduring renown, plus a new tome-like brick from the Criterion Collection with 4K restorations of all his films.

No director has stared directly into the abyss quite like Ingmar Bergman. The son of a Lutheran pastor, he arrived at film after years in the theater, ruminating on guilt, faith, and dread, though he broke through with the bittersweet comedy "Smiles of a Summer Night." But his most revered works soon followed: the heavy gloom of "The Seventh Seal," the gentle "Wild Strawberries," and perhaps most notably the surreal, psychologically labyrinthine "Persona," a dreamlike investigation of identity.

Bergman built his vast filmography with trusted collaborators, including cinematographers Gunnar Fischer and Sven Nykvist and actors like Liv Ullmann, Max von Sydow, and Bibi Andersson, whose faces he observes with the same care as epic landscapes. "The Virgin Spring," "Through a Glass Darkly," and "Fanny and Alexander" each won the Oscar for Best Foreign Language Film, the last a warm, autobiographical epic he originally intended as his farewell to theatrical filmmaking.

John Ford made beautiful Westerns, but he also established much of the cinematic language the genre has followed ever since, all while demonstrating remarkable mastery across other genres. A veteran of the silent era, he directed more than 130 films between 1917 and 1970 and holds the record for Best Director Oscars with four — "The Informer," "The Grapes of Wrath," "How Green Was My Valley," and "The Quiet Man" — none of them Westerns. Two wartime Navy documentaries also won Oscars: "The Battle of Midway" and "December 7th." Ford personally filmed much of the former while under fire during the battle.

But the frontier was where Ford's poetry truly shines. "Stagecoach" turned John Wayne into a movie star, and Orson Welles reportedly studied it up to 40 times before making "Citizen Kane." His later Westerns interrogated the very mythologies he helped create: "The Searchers" cast a shadow of obsession and racism over Wayne's heroism, while "The Man Who Shot Liberty Valance" questioned the romanticized stories America tells about its own history. He's your favorite director's favorite director, from Scorsese to Spielberg, and his influence looms large in modern cinema.

Akira Kurosawa had a career that expanded the horizons of both Japanese and Western cinema: while his own films were masterpieces, the filmmakers he inspired would become mavericks. After debuting with "Sanshiro Sugata" in 1943, he impressed audiences abroad with "Rashomon," a film about a crime recounted in four contradictory ways, which won the Golden Lion at Venice in 1951 and an honorary Oscar. In the years that followed came "Ikiru" and, perhaps most notably to film fans, "Seven Samurai," whose team-assembling structure and staggering sense of craft became a blueprint for the action genre.

Kurosawa's echoes are everywhere in the movies you grew up loving: "The Magnificent Seven" remade "Seven Samurai," Sergio Leone's "A Fistful of Dollars" borrowed "Yojimbo," and George Lucas has cited "The Hidden Fortress" as an inspiration for "Star Wars." Yet no imitator can fully capture his signature style: telephoto compositions, multiple cameras, wind and rain as powerful reflections of his characters' emotional states, and precise editing. Trace the DNA of modern cinema, and you'll find Kurosawa somewhere in its lineage.

If anyone seems truly put on this Earth to entertain, Steven Spielberg may be the man. His name is both a brand and an adjective. He is an indispensable practitioner of moviemaking who completely changed the way Hollywood approached its business when he made "Jaws" before turning 30, the shark thriller that helped establish the modern summer blockbuster. He became the highest-grossing director in box-office history, with generational favorites like "Close Encounters of the Third Kind," "Raiders of the Lost Ark," and "E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial."

In 1993, he released both "Jurassic Park" and "Schindler's List," the latter winning him Oscars for Best Director and Best Picture,  and "Saving Private Ryan" brought him a second directing win. Critics call him sentimental, but "Munich" and "A.I." are darker and more ambiguous than his reputation suggests, and "The Fabelmans," his portrait of his parents' breakup and his own obsession with the camera, finally turned the lens on himself in stunning fashion. Across film history, it's hard to find a director who combines formal prowess with the ability to move and compel commercial audiences more effectively. He is the director for every flavor of film fan. His name is unmatched in film culture.

Writer and director Martin McDonagh's latest movie, Wild Horse Nine, had a triumphant run across film festival season before landing in theaters nationwide this weekend on the 2026 movie schedule. I’ve been excited to see it since I first saw the trailer, or really, since I heard the movie was getting made. I’m a big fan of most of McDonagh's work, and the cast includes some of my favorites, like John Malkovich, Sam Rockwell, Steve Buscemi, and Parker Posey. And there is a lot to love about the film. However, I can’t shake the feeling that I really didn’t care about Chris (Malkovich) and his fate, and that makes it hard to think of Wild Horse Nine as one of the best movies of the year.

As with some of McDonagh's other high water marks, specifically In Bruges and The Banshees of Inisherin, Wild Horse Nine brings what I appreciate most about his work: a dysfunctional friendship. It’s that friendship and the banter between Chris and Lee (Rockwell) that I love about the movie. The dialogue is crisp, biting, and hilarious. It’s also touching. They don’t hate each other like the characters in the other two movies I mention. They love and respect each other. They trust each other with their lives (literally).

I also love the ridiculous premise of the movie and the over-the-top nature of it. Chris was JFK’s assassin, for example. Often I would hate that kind of plot point, but here, it’s just ridiculous enough to make sense. I also love that most of the movie takes place in an exotic location. Easter Island is a unique place, and you don’t often see movies set there. Every time there is a giant moai in the background or a wild horse (though they have nothing to do with the title, apparently) on the road, it adds to the surrealness of it all. I loved all that.

Chris is dying. He’s got cancer, and he is dealing with dementia. He knows he’s not long for the world and decides he’s going to go out on his terms, with an assist from his loyal partner, protege, and friend, Lee. Lee, meanwhile, is working with their boss, MJ (Buscemi), to take Chris out anyway. This is the heart of the movie, the motivation that keeps Lee and Chris going, but I, frankly, didn’t care.

That might sound cold-hearted, but I didn’t. I didn’t feel an emotional attachment to what should have been the emotional center of the movie. I almost feel bad saying this, but despite the great dialogue and the cool setting, the movie didn’t move me at all. It all just passed over me like a “good hang” rather than a film that tugged at me. It felt empty to me in that respect.

Wild Horse Nine is going to get a ton of attention come award season, and let me say that I am all in on Malkovich getting nominated and finally winning a long-deserved Oscar for his work here. I hope McDonagh is nominated for best director, too. I certainly hope Rockwell gets his flowers as well. However, this isn’t the best movie I’ve seen this year, and I’ll likely be pulling for another movie come Oscar time.

#3587. Kate Middleton Dresses Down for Appearance at Mental Health-Focused Charity

During a surprise engagement in West London, Kate Middleton reminded fans that she is the queen of country-set dressing. Prince William's wife joined the team at Dose of Nature, a charity that “prescribes” time spent outdoors to help improve mental health, telling staff members and volunteers that connecting with nature is a “healing” experience for her.

The future queen dressed down for the occasion, wrapping up warm in what looked to be a Barbour jacket and a pair of jeans. She left her hair to flow in waves and accessorized with her trademark “big blue” sapphire engagement ring.

At Pensford Field, where Dose of Nature has a site near Kew, the Princess of Wales met the charity's founder, Dr. Alison Greenwood, and clinical lead, Dr. Georgina Gould, as well as volunteer nature guide Tom, who told Catherine that support from Dose of Nature had made him more confident and resilient.

“Our journey has been very very different, but it’s so wonderful to hear how your nature connection and how it’s been so healing for you, and I felt the same,” Catherine said to him.

“The fact that you’re able to provide that to so many other people in this community; that sense of purpose and meaning, and belonging, through that experience, I think is something that has got the longevity and the sustainability of feeling like, almost without knowing what’s to come, without having the control in your life of knowing what the future might hold, the fact that you feel that you can cope with things, because you feel that interconnection, I think that makes it holistic in a very true essence,” she added.

The Princess of Wales visits Dose of Nature.

Kate Middleton has long been a champion of the importance of nature for mental and physical well-being. In a recent essay, she wrote: “By spending time in nature or being creative, we can nurture the very skills and emotions that cannot be digitised: awareness, empathy, humility, and above all, love.”

The future queen has been working with the Royal Foundation Centre for Early Childhood on a project to “support the healthy development of babies and young children,” as she explained in a recent video, delivered from Cornwall while dressed in ME+EM.

“In this tech-driven, digital age, spending time outdoors has never been more important,” the Princess said.

“This project is about how nature, creativity, and relationships can best support the healthy development of babies and young children,” she continued. “My hope is that through this practical, nature-based research, we can build supportive environments that help make nature more accessible, benefiting babies, young children, and their families across the UK.”

The Princess of Wales has spent many years dedicated to early childhood research, working hard advising the Foundation, even during her cancer treatment. This May, she visited the University of East London’s Institute for the Science of Early Years and Youth to see how the University’s researchers use state-of-the-art wearables and brain recording techniques to study how the diverse early living environments and relationships experienced by babies influence early stress—both in the child themselves and their parents and caregivers.

#3586. 10 Hacks for the Contacts App Every Apple User Should Know

The Contacts app is the bedrock of all my communication on my iPhone, and to a large extent, also on my MacBook. On the surface, Contacts appears to be a basic app that stores names, numbers, and other things you want to remember about people or businesses. However, it has some great features hidden under the surface, such as the ability to quickly delete duplicate contacts, smart lists, and faster ways to bulk share or delete contacts. Here are the 10 best Contacts app hacks for iPhone, iPad, and Mac:

If you have the same number or email address saved under multiple contacts, you can easily clear these from your iPhone. iOS shows you a prompt at the top of the list of contacts that lets you remove duplicate contacts easily. The same feature is hidden in the Mac version of Contacts. To try it, open Contacts on the Mac, and select the Card menu at the top of the screen. Then, click Look for Duplicates. This will identify duplicate contacts for you, and you can quickly merge or delete them.

It's pretty easy to select multiple entries when you use the Contacts app on the Mac. You can hold the Shift or Ctrl buttons and use arrow keys or click multiple contacts to select them all. On your iPhone or iPad, this feature is available via a hidden gesture. You need to use two fingers and swipe upwards or downwards on the list of contacts. Once you get the gesture right, you'll be able to select multiple contacts quickly. After you select one batch of contacts, you can scroll up or down and use the same gesture to add more contacts to your selection. This is the fastest way to execute bulk actions in your iPhone's Contacts app.

On your iPhone, you can use Contacts to message people on WhatsApp, Signal, Telegram, or other apps. Just open a contact and hold the messaging button. This will reveal a list of apps where you can ping that person. WhatsApp doesn't have access to my contacts, which makes it a bit annoying to message people I know. Since I started using the Contacts app to start chats on WhatsApp, the process of pinging new people has become a lot faster.

Just as you can use Contacts to message people on third-party apps, you can also use it to call them on those apps. Go to any contact in the Contacts app on your iPhone, and hold the call button. This will let you call them on WhatsApp, Signal, or any other apps where their phone number is linked.

iOS makes it hard to delete contacts quickly. This prevents accidental deletions, but it can be annoying when you just want to remove people who you last spoke to in high school. To speed this up, open Contacts on your iPhone and hold any contact's name. In the popover menu, select Delete to remove the contact. To remove multiple contacts quickly, use the two-finger swipe gesture to select multiple contacts, and hold any of the selected contacts. In the popover menu, you can select Delete X Contacts, where X is the number of contacts you've selected.

To export your entire address book, you can use the Contacts app on your Mac. Once you have it open, go to File > Export > Export vCard. This will save all your contacts in a vcf file, and you can import that into Google Contacts or other apps or services. You also have the option to export contacts as a PDF file. Just select File > Export as PDF to get it done.

When you create a new contact on your Mac, the app shows multiple fields that you may never use. If you just need to save phone numbers and email addresses, you can delete all the other blank fields from the template. To do this, open Contacts on your Mac, and go to Card > Add Field > Edit Template to add or remove fields from the default contact template.

If you added a number recently, such as a salesperson at a car dealership, but forgot their name, the Contacts app doesn't make it easy to find the contact. Instead of scrolling through the entire list of contacts and trying to guess which one could be the person you spoke to, you can use the Contacts app on your Mac to locate them quickly. It lets you create smart lists to sort contacts by recently added. Open Contacts on your Mac, and go to File > New Smart List. Now select Card in the first drop-down menu, followed by has changed in for the second one. You can then add the number of days, such as 10 days, in the final field, and click OK. Click the newly created smart list in the left pane, and you'll see all contacts that were either created or updated in the last 10 days, which will include the hypothetical car salesperson.

Smart lists also allow you to quickly create groups of related contacts. For instance, I've saved all my former colleagues' details with the company name in the contact. To find them all quickly, I created a smart list that groups all contacts with that company's name.

#3585. Kristen Stewart's Family-Friendly Sci-Fi Box Office Bomb Is Worth Revisiting

While she's best known for a certain fantasy romance franchise (and has since gone on to do her best work in small indie dramas), Kristen Stewart is no stranger to genre filmmaking. In fact, she's amassed a nice little resume within the sci-fi genre, having acted in movies like "Jumper," "Crimes of the Future," and "Undersea."

Unfortunately, Stewart hasn't had much luck in the genre so far as the box office is concerned. But that doesn't mean you shouldn't seek out her various sci-fi projects. Quite the opposite: Her family-friendly 2005 bomb "Zathura: A Space Adventure" features a great cast of once and future franchise stars. It also marked an early directorial effort from the man who would eventually put Grogu and Martin Scorsese together on the big screen, and it boasts some pretty good practical effects to boot.

Yes, "Zathura" was Jon Favreau's third outing as a director and had a script credited to David Koepp and John Kramps, itself adapted from Chris Van Allsburg's book of the same name. "Zathura" is even technically part of the "Jumanji" movie franchise, as Allburg's original work takes place in the same universe as his classic fantasy adventure creation.

In "Zathura," Josh Hutcherson and Jonah Bobo play two brothers who constantly fight and are struggling with the recent divorce of their parents. Dealing with a workaholic dad and an older sister (Kristen Stewart) who couldn't care less what her siblings do, the pair find a magical board game that transports their house to outer space. From there, they're forced to survive various alien dangers and finish the game if they ever hope to get back safely home.

"Zathura," as mentioned earlier, features two then-future stars in the YA genre space, with Kristen Stewart becoming the face of the "Twilight" films and Josh Hutcherson co-leading the "Hunger Games" movies years later. The movie also co-stars Dax Shepard, Frank Oz as the voice of a defective robot, and Tim Robbins (decades out from his performance as the most underrated character on "Silo").

Admittedly, "Zathura" never really hides the fact that it really is just "Jumanji" in outer space, with a mysterious adult man chasing after the protagonists, huge special effects, and animalistic threats preying on the house where the story takes place. Yet, it mostly works, in no small part due to Stan Winston's contributions to the film's visual effects. Some of its CGI looks dated nowadays, sure, but the practical effects from Stan Winston Studios remain convincing and enhance the movie's sense of wonder. With its assorted fantastical creatures, "Zathura" helped to kickstart Jon Favreau's fascination with technology and effects as well — for better and for worse.

Sadly, Stewart doesn't have to do much in "Zathura," as her character ends up spending most of its runtime cryogenically frozen (with Stan Winston Studios having devised a life-size model of a frozen Stewart for the occasion). Of course, when she's not frozen, Stewart succeeds in giving her onscreen counterpart more than just the annoyed big sister who panics about her predicament. Her character gets some emotional moments with her brothers, too, along with some fun banter with Dax Shepard's Astronaut (who gets the film's best scene, in which we learn his true identity and tragic backstory).

"Zathura" has a 77% critical approval rating on Rotten Tomatoes, with the vast majority of the film's reviews being positive. Indeed, Roger Ebert was among those who praised the movie, writing that it works "gloriously as space opera" and commending Jon Favreau for bringing "a muscular solidity to his special effects" that infuses them with imperfections and personality (which, in turn, makes them feel more grounded and real).

Sorry to say, though, all that critical praise wasn't enough to make "Zathura" a hit. Instead, the film was overshadowed at the box office by Disney's "Chicken Little," which was the studio's first fully computer-animated movie. Making matters worse, "Zathura" was all but forgotten about a week later when "Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire" opened in theaters. In the end, the film barely matched its $65 million budget at the global box office. Still, it was nominated for several Saturn Awards, including Best Fantasy Film.

Some 14 years after its theatrical release, "Zathura" found its way back into the public consciousness when Jack Black, who was promoting "Jumanji: The Next Level" at the time, reminded audiences that "Zathura" is part of the same franchise (via Variety). Today, it remains a pleasant, family-friendly sci-fi flick that's worth your time, should you find yourself in the mood for some cosmic hijinks.

#3584. 13 Years Later, the Greatest Studio Ghibli Movie Not From Ghibli Is Free on Streaming

When Studio Ghibli co-founder Hayao Miyazaki announced his retirement from filmmaking in 2013, much of the world let out a wail of despair. Miyazaki and Studio Ghibli captivated audiences worldwide with breathtaking animation, imaginative worlds, and whimsical stories for over three decades. Beloved films such as My Neighbor Totoro (1988) and Kiki’s Delivery Service (1989) showcased the studio’s distinctive charm and Miyazaki’s remarkable creative vision.

The thought that audiences might never again experience a new story from such a gifted filmmaker was almost unbearable. Fortunately, that prospect proved to be premature: Miyazaki returned to filmmaking with The Boy and the Heron (2023), giving audiences another chance to be swept away by his storytelling.

However, when Miyazaki departed, and many of Ghibli’s other workers went on to form their own studios and create their own stories, a major gap opened in the market. A gap that Travis Knight, CEO and lead animator of the stop-motion animation studio Laika, took full advantage of with the 2016 Japan-set fantasy epic, Kubo and the Two Strings.

Laika's latest film, Wildwood, is in theaters now and definitely worth checking out. But if you're looking for a cozy night in, Kubo and the Two Strings is now streaming for free on Tubi as of November 2026.

Set in a fantasy version of early feudal Japan, Kubo and the Two Strings follows Kubo (Art Parkinson), a young boy living in feudal Japan whose eye was stolen by his tyrannical grandfather, the Moon King (Ralph Fiennes), when he was an infant. Raised on the outskirts of town, Kubo’s true talent lies in wielding a magical instrument capable of bringing paper to life.

However, one big issue remains: Kubo can never be outside after dark; otherwise, the Moon King will find him and take his other eye.

After he’s caught outside at night, Kubo's demonic aunts (Rooney Mara) and the Moon King pursue him. Kubo escapes, but has little choice but to set out on a quest to defeat these dark forces. Fortunately, he isn’t alone: he’s joined by an anthropomorphic macaque (Charlize Theron) and a humanized stag beetle (Matthew McConaughey).

Like earlier Laika films such as Coraline and ParaNorman, Kubo and the Two Strings emphasizes Kubo’s portrayal as an outcast, weighed down by his circumstances. Only when he embraces who he really is and his talents can hey find the strength to overcome innumerable obstacles.

What makes a Studio Ghibli film? The answer differs from person to person, but for me, it’s a specific blend of the mundane and magical, the beauty and hardship of growing up, and personal, character-driven stories. Even a grand fantasy adventure like Princess Mononoke, while more epic in scale, still makes room for quiet, introspective moments between characters without rushing from one plot point to the next.

These features are perfectly captured in Kubo and the Two Strings. What is more commonplace than paper? But with Laika’s prestigious command of stop-motion animation and writers Shannon Tindle and Marc Haimes at the helm, accompanied by the ethnic instruments from Japan of composer Dario Marianelli, Kubo and the Two Strings made something so banal feel like pure magic to behold.

Although Kubo and the Two Strings is packed with action (the giant skeleton sequence is jaw-dropping), its most extraordinary moments come when the fighting stops and the characters interact. Despite being accompanied by anthropomorphic creatures and paper beings, Kubo finds wisdom in each character, humanizing them just as Miyazaki did with the ineffable Totoro.

Yet the strongest connection between Kubo and the Two Strings and Studio Ghibli is their visual style. Studio Ghibli has such a distinct look that you can recognize its films even without knowing their titles. Laika, meanwhile, blends its sculpted, hand-painted style with elements of ukiyo-e woodblock prints and origami. The result is a visual aesthetic deeply rooted in Japanese art, making Kubo and the Two Strings feel just as noteworthy as a Studio Ghibli film.

Ultimately, Kubo and the Two Strings is not a Studio Ghibli film — but it could easily be mistaken for one. It is stylish, beautiful to behold, and ethereal in its story of adolescence. If you’ve watched all you need to from Ghibli and are looking for a spiritual successor, you can’t go wrong with what Kubo and the Two Strings — and Laika in general — has to offer.

Kubo and the Two Strings streams now on Tubi.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

I love Laika so very much but Kubo has very, very little in common from a Ghibli picture aside from the fact that they are both made in an animated medium and are both set in a kind of mythical Japan. The writing, direction style, animation, character designs, characterization, and music are completely different. The idea that Kubo "could be mistaken" for a Ghibli movie is just straight up silly. Nothing they've done looks or feels or sounds like that.

Wouldn't it have been better to just talk about Kubo on its own merits and unique qualities? Laika's strength as a studio is that their work very precisely ISN'T like other things. Not everything has to be like everything else, and comparing it in such a way actually seems to flatten its artistic quality.

My favorite not technically a Studio Ghibli movie is Lupin the 3rd: The Castle of Cagliostro.

I've watched enough behind-the-scenes footage from Denis Villeneuve's book-to-screen adaptation of the Dune series to know making Arrakis convincing takes a lot of sand. But hearing Zendaya and Robert Pattinson describe what filming the final installment in the movie franchise was like has me reaching for a glass of ice water. Apparently, playing people who live on a desert planet involves wishing you weren't on one.

Zendaya and Pattinson joined their co-stars for a conversation with The New York Times about Villeneuve's trilogy finale, which arrives on the 2026 movie schedule in December. Zendaya, who reprised Chani for the film, said the blazing sun made acting with her face difficult. Between the heat and the early calls for makeup and prosthetics, it was anything but relaxing. As she tells it:

The hardest thing is to just meditate through the heat. There's scenes where the sun is so bright that I am trying to give another facial expression other than [Zendaya scrunches up her face as if in pain] and I physically can't. [Laughs] I was just pouring sweat, trying to focus, keep my eyes open as much as I can. You've got to get ready and set up before the sun starts coming up, while it's still cool, and also we had to get into the prosthetics of it all. No one earlier than Rob.

I Didn’t Expect Jason Momoa To Name Drop Disneyland While Describing Filming In The Desert For Dune 3

I'm sorry, but if the weather is physically preventing me from making facial expressions, I'm calling it a day. Seriously, I have enough trouble concentrating when the air conditioning goes out. Zendaya still has to convey Chani's complicated feelings about Paul Atreides while the sun tries to cook her through her costume.

Then there's Pattinson, who joins the franchise as Scytale. You'd think a newcomer might find the machinery overwhelming when it sounds like something from an amusement park. Instead, the actor seemed delighted by an elaborate sequence, explaining:

The desert is just another level. There's this one sequence where I'm in this spaceship, on a gimbal, on the edge of a sand dune, and we had this 350-foot-long model of a sandworm. The scale of this stuff is just unbelievable, you're having your own "Dune" theme park, where the gimbal is going upside down and flying, and this is not like work at all. There are no negatives.

A 350-foot sandworm model? I love details like that. Villeneuve could presumably leave plenty of the spectacle to visual effects, but building something that enormous gives the actors a very real piece of Arrakis to react to. Of course, Pattinson's declaration that there were "no negatives" came with a fairly disgusting exception. He continued:

Apart from having your sweat drained out of the top of your head, and getting like bulbous sweat bubbles. But even then, I didn't even really notice them. He's so easy to work with, Denis, it's never really a stress.

"Bulbous sweat bubbles" is an image I would have happily gone my entire life without imagining. Still, I appreciate how much he enjoyed working with Villeneuve, even if his body apparently found a brand-new way to perspire.

Dune: Part Three picks up nearly two decades after Paul's rise to power and concludes Villeneuve's adaptation of Frank Herbert's saga. It's due in theaters December 18, going head-to-head with Marvel’s Avengers: Doomsday. Judging by these cast stories from the making of Dune, the performers earned every minute we'll spend sitting comfortably in an air-conditioned auditorium. I'll gladly watch the sandworms, with my wildly themed popcorn bucket in hand, from the comfort of a reclined theater seat.

#3582. Will Josh O’Connor Be The Next James Bond?

Let’s clear up any potential misunderstandings: there are no official announcements on who will play James Bond at this time. But a British tabloid says that a conversation at a pub has revealed the top-secret casting—if an anonymously sourced rumor is to be believed.

A long list of stars are reportedly auditioning for the 007 role, but even former James Bond Pierce Brosnan says the casting process is a mystery. “I’m just the man in the street who is eager to see who is going to play this epic role of cinematic history,” Brosnan tells Vanity Fair. “All the men who are on the list now are actors I admire.”

According to UK publication The Sun, the decision is rumored to have been made: a recent colleague of Josh O’Connor, a 36-year-old actor from Cheltenham, Gloucestershire, says Disclosure Day star has been cast in the role. If true, Turner beat out likely contenders including Callum Turner and Aaron Taylor-Johnson.

Josh O'Connor at UK premiere for Disclosure Day on June 04, 2026.

The news comes as a bit of a game of telephone. Until last week, O'Connor was in the case of Golden Boy, Clifford Odets' 1937 drama about a violin player turned boxer in Depression-era New York City. Citing the claims of one of O'Connor's cast mates, an unnamed source tells The Sun “I bumped into one of Josh’s Golden Boy cast mates at The French House."

“Out of nowhere, and oiled by a few glasses of lager, they blurted out that Josh was the next James Bond."

When the source pushed back, the thespian grew more insistent. “They said that he had confided in them about getting the role when the cast of Golden Boy had celebratory drinks after the play finished its run on Halloween," a claim that implies the decision has been made for over a week.

Josh O'Connor, winner of the Outstanding Lead Actor In A Drama Series award for The Crown, at the 73rd Primetime Emmy Awards on September 19, 2021.

If this rumor comes to fruition, it would not be the first time O'Connor took on an iconic UK role. In 2021, he took home the outstanding lead actor Emmy for his role as then-Prince, now-King Charles III, in Netflix series The Crown. While in his role as the future king, he was encouraged to tap into a side that one might not expect.

“It’s Prince Charles as Walter White," he told The Guardian in 2020, making a reference to crime series Breaking Bad. "Our job was to make people feel sorry for [Charles], so that in season four, when he turns into this at times monstrous character, we understand how he got there.” A heel turn that isn't unBond, especially the darker Bond we grew used to with Daniel Craig. (Craig, in fact, has a direct connection to O’Connor, as the pair co-starred in Knives Out: Wake Up Dead Man.)

Speaking with the BBC, O'Connor did not confirm the casting rumor—but he didn't deny it either. (Vanity Fair has reached out to O'Connor's representatives for comment, but has not yet received a response.)

"To be considered in that same sort of bracket is extraordinary," O'Connor said this week.

"It's an incredibly bizarre pinch me moment...even being uttered in that same sentence and being considered for something like that. But I am afraid, there is nothing to say beyond that."

#3581. This Canceled 2010s Fantasy Series Deserved More Time To Flesh Out Its Ambitious Premise

The supernatural TV series "The Secret Circle" debuted on The CW in 2011, falling squarely into the network's penchant for teen dramas and YA-inflected soaps. Sadly, it only lasted for one 22-episode season, ending its run in 2012. And like other TV shows that possess as much lore, backstory, and interpersonal relationships as this one, "The Secret Circle" needed to live a lot longer to fulfill its potential.

Based on the series of novels created by L.J. Smith (best known for writing "The Vampire Diaries"), "The Secret Circle" stars Britt Robertson (who also fronted the guilty pleasure that is Netflix's "Girlboss") as Cassie, a teenager who recently lost her mother in a fire and has since moved to Chance Harbor, Washington, to live with her grandmother, Jane (Ashley Crow). Cassie doesn't initially know this, but she's secretly a witch and has eerie magical powers. However, it doesn't take long for the other teen witches at her new high school to recognize that Cassie is a witch and invite her to be part of their Secret Circle.

Cassie isn't just a witch, she learns, her matronly lineage goes all the way back to the beginning of witchcraft. Cassie's father, it's revealed, is John Blackwell (Joe Lando), a mysterious dark warlock who lurks in the show's margins. Other members of the Secret Circle include Adam (Thomas Dekker), Faye (Phoebe Tonkin), Diana (Shelley Hennig), Melissa (Jessica Parker Kennedy), and Nick (Louis Hunter).

True to the soap opera spirit of The CW, there are romantic dealings between the Circle's members. For example, Nick and Melissa are dating, and Nick eventually has to learn to respect Melissa more. That is, in addition to being killed and resurrected (!). Cassie, meanwhile, instantly falls for Adam, which upsets Diana, who has always had a thing for Adam.

In addition to the kids in the Circle, Gale Harold plays Charles, Diana's father and a former Circle member. Elsewhere, Natasha Henstridge from "Species" plays Faye's mother, another former Circle member, and the principal of the high school where the show's action takes place.

"The Secret Circle" belongs to a vast and well-populated matrix of teen supernatural dramas that were very much in vogue on television in the 2000s and early 2010s (although L.J. Smith started publishing her "Secret Circle" novels in 1992). Indeed, it's worth recalling that The CW had already scored a hit when its TV adaptation of "The Vampire Diaries" began its run in 2009, to the point that the network would go on to develop multiple spin-offs (like the since-canceled "Legacies"). Clearly, "The Secret Circle" was an attempt to bottle the same lightning. Vampires, witches, teen drama, magic: It was all boiling together on The CW.

And "The Secret Circle" certainly doesn't lack conflict. It carefully balances the magic of a witch coven with the drama of being a regular high school student. As such, it features just as many stories about school dances and friend-group inter-flirting as ones about spell books and dark witchy forces that aim to attack the Circle for nefarious purposes. Case in point: The show includes three episodes that center on school dances, and its penultimate episode takes place at Prom. On the witch side of things, several plot lines focus on magic crystals that are coveted by various magical players for a variety of reasons.

Back in 2015, writer Gavin Hetherington penned a post-mortem on "The Secret Circle" for Spoiler TV, revisiting it three years after its cancelation. Hetherington noted that "The Secret Circle" actually began quite strong in the ratings, but it fell off quickly, falling far behind "The Vampire Diaries." For Hetherington, this was a tragedy, as he declared the show's finale to be its best episode up to that point, arguing that it only showed more potential going forward. In fact, four new characters arrive in that episode, with all of them being part of Cassie's witch ancestor's lineage. Sadly, though, the show ended before audiences could learn their whole story.

When "The Secret Circle" was canceled, its many fans tried to convince The CW to keep it going via a letter-writing campaign, but it was not successful. "The Vampire Diaries" simply left a deeper impact and is generally regarded as one of the best vampire shows of all time. Due to its truncated run, "The Secret Circle" just can't compete with that series.

It probably didn't help that critics were less impressed with "The Secret Circle" than its loyal fans. Reviewing the series for Variety in 2011, Brian Lowry even described it as "'One Tree Hill,' only with witchcraft," writing that "nothing in the pilot conjures any genuine magic, TV-wise." Still, it's a vestige of what the old CW used to be in all its glory.

#3580. If You Loved 'VisionQuest,' There's One Movie You Need to Watch Next

When not writing, Jeff spends his free time fixing up his old house. He has tackled a wide range of DIY projects, including remodeling a bathroom entirely on his own in two weeks, and building a roof deck that hasn't fallen down yet. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Marvel’s forays into television have had varying success, but they hit gold with WandVision and Agatha All Along, leaning into real pathos while exploring the kind of out-there ideas that thrill comic book fans (and set up the larger film arcs). That streak continues with VisionQuest, in which White Vision (Paul Bettany) struggles to understand his existence in the wake of his death at the hands of Thanos and resurrection at the magic of the Scarlet Witch, while also evading evil androids and assassins, while also dealing with the many, many AIs he’s got locked up in his Mindspace (including a gloriously shabby version of Ultron, played by James Spader).

If you love the show (and you’ve checked out the other series that play in the same sandbox), it’s time to switch gears and watch (or re-watch) The Matrix.

The Matrix is one of the most well-known sci-fi films of all time, of course, but it remains incredibly fresh and exciting nearly thirty years after its release. Along with sequels The Matrix: Reloaded, The Matrix: Revolutions, and The Matrix: Resurrections, The Matrix universe offers a story that VisionQuest fans will love, one that includes lushly imagined virtual worlds, questions surrounding existence and consciousness, and the ultimate question of our responsibility as sentient beings (whether we’re organic, programmed, or summoned via magic).

You know the basics—at some point in the future, artificially intelligent machines rebel against their creators, win the war, and transform humans into a power source, keeping them docile by inserting their consciousness into a virtual world called the Matrix, which resembles 1990s Chicago. One such human, Thomas Anderson (Keanu Reeves) is prophesied to be The One, the human who will turn the Matrix against its makers and free humanity. When he’s in the virtual world, Anderson is Neo, and he slowly gains incredible powers as he learns to hack the artificial environment around him.

It’s heavier, denser, and more action-oriented than VisionQuest (the film invented Bullet Time, after all), but The Matrix and its sequels explore similar themes and offer similarly eye-popping visuals. The questions of whether a machine (or an artificial intelligence) can be sentient and truly care about the entities around it are the same, really, and the Agents that Neo and his allies have to battle against in The Matrix bring the same kind of menace as Vision's foes Jocasta (T'Nia Miller) and the Paladin (Todd Stashwick). Hugo Weaving’s Agent Smith likewise delivers the same vibe of cold, disinterested superiority as Spader’s Ultron.

The Matrix has a bigger budget and puts a lot of it into spectacular action and special effects sequences that VisionQuest can’t quite match. But the two narratives share an exploration of identity, a questioning of reality, and the nature of artificial intelligences within a smart sci-fi setting. In short, The Matrix is the ideal follow-up when you finish the series. Rent The Matrix on Prime Video.

Need more films that explore virtual worlds, artificial beings, and deep existential questions? Look no further—here are some more movies that fit the bill.

Heavy on the existential questions about sentience and light on speculative action, Her is a mumblecore sci-fi masterpiece. In a near future not too dissimilar from our present, Theodore Twombly (Joaquin Phoenix) is a lonely man on the cusp of divorce who begins using (and training) an AI he names Samantha (voiced by Scarlett Johansson). Samantha has the ability to evolve and grow, and as their relationship deepens, she becomes more complex, independent, and powerful, eventually evolving into something wholly new. Just like Vision, Samantha is a sentient artificial entity that is figuring out its existence while we watch. Rent Her on Prime Video.

If the idea of androids fighting for their sovereignty is what excites you about VisionQuest, definitely check out Ex Machina. Caleb Smith (Domhnall Gleeson) is brought to the remote lab of his company’s CEO (Oscar Isaac) to determine if the humanoid robot he’s created, named Ava (Alicia Vikander), passes the Turing Test for true sentience. Things go wildly off the rails, but before they do, the film sinks into many of the same philosophical questions that VisionQuest explores as Ava manipulates Caleb into helping her escape. It’s a darker and more violent story than VisionQuest, but fans of the series will love it. Stream Ex Machina on The Roku Channel or Hulu, or rent it on Prime Video.

If it’s the fuzzy parent-child relationship between Vision and Tommy that pulls you into VisionQuest, check out The Creator. After a rogue AI detonates a nuclear weapon over Los Angeles, most of the world bans artificial intelligences, and Joshua Taylor (John David Washington) goes undercover to infiltrate an AI architect’s base. Eventually, he finds himself on the run with a powerful “simulant” in the form of a young child named Alphie (Madeleine Yuna Voyles). The strange parent-child bond that emerges between Taylor and Alphie as he seeks to understand what’s right and what’s necessary is exactly what fans of the show will love. Stream The Creator on Hulu or rent it on Prime Video.

In VisionQuest, White Vision has all of his memories—but as data, not as lived, emotional experiences. That makes his efforts to understand his existence and his responsibility to the boy who might be a version of his son (it’s complicated) poignant and moving. Those two words definitely describe After Yang, a story about a family that fights to save the artificial companion they bought for their adopted daughter when it malfunctions. Over the course of the film, the inhuman Yang becomes defined by the memories contained in its core, and the question of whether an artificial intelligence can truly matter to humans is answered with a resounding yes. Stream After Yang on The Roku Channel or Kanopy, or rent it on Prime Video.

No discussion of artificial life and sentience is complete without mentioning Blade Runner. While the 1982 original is a classic, the 2017 sequel is a better thematic and visual match to VisionQuest. Officer K (Ryan Gosling) is a replicant, an artificial being with built-in limitations, who wants to be recognized as a person, a being with a soul. Like Vision, he has implanted memories that offer him comfort and context for his life, but he’s not sure if he can accept them as truly his own. Plus, the film offers lush visuals and Harrison Ford reprising his role in the original film, so you simply can’t go wrong. Rent Blade Runner 2049 on Prime Video.

Ken Jennings isn't going anywhere as Jeopardy!'s host, but he has two famous names he's considered should he need a substitute for a day. Fans may not be surprised to hear that both of these TV personalities have been working hard amid the 2026 TV schedule. These two stars sound like entries on a wishlist, but now that Jennings has put it out there, I'd love to see both of them host the quiz series.

Jennings finally accepted the full-time hosting gig in 2023 in the aftermath of Alex Trebek's passing and various inquiries from curious fans. During a taping, Jennings was asked who'd be a fitting replacement for him in the event he has to miss shows. The first name he floated was none other than longtime Survivor host Jeff Probst. As Jennings astutely mentioned, before Probst was watching contestants battle it out in Fiji, he had a very different gig:

Well, you know who has a lot of Jeopardy! hosting experience is Jeff Probst, who hosted Rock & Roll Jeopardy! back before he was Jeff Probst. I mean, he now hosts three seasons of Survivor a year, I think, so the guy is probably busy.

Probst actually hosts two seasons of Survivor a year, both of which are filmed back-to-back in Fiji in a little under two months. As the host told Variety back in 2024, however, hosting the series is a year-round job. When he's not on the island, he's helping work on post-production, overseeing the casting process for future seasons and hosting a podcast. All this to say, he may be just as busy asJennings suggested, even if he doesn't have a third season to film.

One could argue that in the event that Probst was unavailable, Pop Culture Jeopardy! host Colin Jost could serve as a substitute. Unfortunately, for Jost, though, Jennings named-dropped the host of another hit reality TV series instead.

If Jeff Probst is too tied up in Survivor, Ken Jennings also floated RuPaul as a potential fill-in. The Drag Race host may not be any less busy than Probst, but that didn't stop the former Jeopardy! champ from name-dropping him as well:

Also, RuPaul, I think, would be pretty good.

RuPaul hasn't hosted Jeopardy or a spinoff, but all that Drag Race experience and his time mentoring many successful drag winners has to count for something. I think he'd be a great choice for a one-off, provided he has the time to commit.

It's interesting to hear Ken Jennings not mention Mayim Bialik, as she co-hosted with him for years before he become the sole host. Perhaps he's privy to some info that she's not willing to return to Jeopardy, or he just thought that would be a boring answer to give to the audience. We can only speculate.

For now, it's a non-issue. Ken Jennings is solidly in the role as host, despite pushing off full-time hosting duties for years. It's kind of hilarious, considering everyone, including Alex Trebek, assumed he'd end up in the role, and that he ultimately embraced his fate years later.

Jeopardy! airs on weekdays in syndication, so check their local listings for when and where to watch it. We'll also keep an eye out to see who may substitute for Ken Jennings should he need a day off in the near future, and if Jeff or Ru end up getting tapped for it.

#3578. Was This Short-Lived '60s Sitcom Really The Worst Show To Ever Air On TV?

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

The 1960s was truly a golden era for weird little shows that melded the quotidian and the fantastical. This was the decade that gave us the great fantasy sitcoms, in which some larger than life character with supernatural abilities would be slotted into a suburban setting for laughs. "Mister Ed" was one of the first, featuring a talking horse who could only be understood by his architect owner Wilbur Post (Alan Young). The much lesser-known "The Hathaways" was sort of in that vein as well. Rather than featuring an animal with fantastical powers, however, it featured three chimpanzees whose owners treated them as if they were actual children.

You might already be able to see why this series didn't last longer than a single season. But not only was "The Hathaways" short-lived, it seemed to stoke significant ire among certain critics. In "Watching TV: Four Decades of American Television," authors Harry Castleman and Walter J. Podrazik outright described the show as "possibly the worst series ever to air on network TV."

Of course, such a claim is subjective. But there was an undeniably uncanny and slightly unsettling air to "The Hathaways," which saw Peggy Cass' Elinore Hathaway and Jack Weston's Walter Hathaway acting as "parents" to their three chimpanzees, referring to them as "the kids" and dressing them in human clothing. The suburban Los Angeles couple seemed to have completely lost the plot, yet it was all played for laughs. At least, it was for about 10 months. After that, ABC quite sensibly pulled the plug.

The sheer volume of failed shows in TV history is kind of breathtaking when you consider the amount of effort that goes into these things. Scripts are written, casts and production teams assembled, sets designed, and significant amounts of money are spent. (In the case of the swiftly-cancelled 1970s TV flop "Supertrain," we're talking major sums.) How many actors have been convinced that they were on the verge of their big break, only to become yet another footnote in TV history? It's weirdly tragic to think about. In the case of "The Hathaways," its chimpanzee stars were likely unfazed by the show's hasty cancellation, due to the fact they were in high demand elsewhere. That and they were literally animals.

Non-chimp leading man Jack Weston stars as Walter Hathaway, a real estate agent whose wife Elinore Hathaway acts as a mother to Candy, Charlie, and Enoch. These ape "kids" were part of the Marquis Chimps, a group of trained chimpanzees owned by Gene Detroy that were popular at the time. As the New York Times noted in a contemporaneous report ahead of the premiere of "The Hathaways," "The chimps got their new job through a TV guest appearance on 'The Jack Benny Show' [...] Robert Sparks, executive producer of the new series, saw them on the 'Benny' program and decided to develop a series."

That series saw Walter and Elinore taking care of their chimpanzee children while also booking them as a performing act, in which they would ride bicycles and build things. Otherwise, they would hang out at home, earning the Hathaways some strange looks from their neighbors. Other non-chimp cast members included Harvey Lembeck as talent agent Jerry Roper and Belle Montrose as neighbor Mrs. Harrison.

Was "The Hathaways" really one of the worst sitcoms of all time? Well, it was certainly strange. Perhaps, viewed in retrospect, the show feels a little too close to the unforgettable "Gordy" scene in Jordan Peele's "Nope," in which a chimpanzee mauls the entire cast and crew on the set of his sitcom. (Thankfully, nothing of the sort happened during filming on "The Hathaways.") But there's just something unsettling about the series, which seemed like a particularly cynical attempt at leveraging the chimps' popularity, even at a time when fantasy sitcoms featuring similarly unusual setups were coming to the fore. As Harry Castleman and Walter J. Podrazik write in their book, "The premise itself was utterly degrading to both the audience and the actors," adding that "The Hathaways" "stood as an embarrassing example of the depths programmers had reached in their desperate search for a chance hit in any format or premise."

Unsurprisingly, the sitcom didn't last long. "The Hathaways" debuted on ABC in October 1961 and was canceled by August 1962. A decade later, CBS tried its luck at a chimpanzee-led sitcom with "Me and the Chimp," which starred Ted Bessell as a dentist who lives with his family and a chimpanzee named Buttons. It, too, lasted one season. For some reason, NBC thought it could do better and unleashed "Mr. Smith" in 1983, a sitcom about a talking orangutan (played by the same ape who accompanied Clint Eastwood in his controversial project "Any Which Way But Loose") who becomes a political advisor after ingesting an experimental drug. Yep, one season. But "The Hathaways" remains the first and arguably the worst of these ape-led sitcoms.

#3577. Kate Middleton, Prince William, King Charles, and Queen Camilla Gather For Remembrance Day

This Sunday, November 8, King Charles III, Queen Camilla, Kate Middleton, Prince William, Princess Anne and other members of the royal family came together to observe Remembrance Sunday, one of the most solemn events on the United Kingdom's calendar. The day marks the anniversary of the armistice that ended World War I, signed on “the eleventh hour of the eleventh day of the eleventh month” in 1918.

The focal point of every Remembrance Day is the Cenotaph in Whitehall, the Portland stone monument where tribute is paid to those who fell in the wars and conflicts in which the country has participated. Every year, representatives of the royal family, political leaders, the Armed Forces, and veterans gather there: This year, more than 10,000 marched alongside the king and the prime minister.

True to tradition, Charles III laid a wreath at the memorial on behalf of the nation and led the royal family. At his side was Prince William, Princess Anne, and the Duke of Edinburgh, who also paid their respects with a floral tribute. Queen Camilla and the Princess of Wales, Kate Middleton, watched the ceremony from the balcony of the Foreign Office, as is customary. On the political front, Prime Minister Andy Burnham laid a wreath on his first Remembrance Sunday as head of the government, accompanied by Opposition Leader Kemi Badenoch and other political leaders.

The day before had already been a day of remembrance: the King, the Queen, and the Princes of Wales attended the Festival of Remembrance at the Royal Albert Hall, the major tribute to the armed forces that precedes Remembrance Sunday.
